Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Gold Peak Worthy, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The matter lies in the meeting of lid and box; the principle should meet like the points of arrows.
If you can speak it, I will divide half the monastery with you. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed. Gold Peak said, "It is easy to get along when we first meet;
it is difficult to live together as one man. He then descended from his seat. The Master remarked: "Gold Peak’s letting go was too light; his gathering in was too heavy."
"Coming here is too much. Huilin said, "It is not so. Not seeing any phrases at all, he blinds the eyes of people of this age.
If you can speak, then why mention dividing the monastery into halves? I shall entrust everything—the bowl and the bag—to you all at once.
After a long silence, he said, "What need is there to seek white jade? This very thing is gold."
Ascending the hall, he said: "This year, for the second time, we have met the Double Fifth Festival. There is no need to beat the drum for the boat race anymore.
Outside the Gate of Vajra, there is laughter; throughout the night, sweat poured from his entire body like rain. Sweat like rain—no words are needed. Even the rhinoceros fan is in vain.
On the old mountain, much snow has accumulated; when will I return?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "An ancient said, 'A foot of practice is better than ten feet of talk;
an inch of practice is better than a foot of talk; a fraction of practice is better than an inch of talk.
Furthermore, a venerable master said, 'Speak that which cannot be practiced; practice that which cannot be spoken. Although it is thus, it is not yet..."
Exempted from accompanying others, one remains apart. Now tell me: how does one act when there are no words to be spoken? Speech that does not wound others is what issues forth;
medicine is passed on to others only once its efficacy has been proven.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.
Śākyamuni the Old Man knew only the first half, but not the second: "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body; within it there is neither defilement nor dust.
When picking up the spoon and grasping the chopsticks, one is as clear as day; sweeping the floor and burning incense, one acts with such clarity.
He did not seek the assistance of others.
At Nengren Monastery in Jiangning, a monk was dispatched with a formal letter to invite the head seat Quan to take charge of the monastery. Quan firmly refused to accept.
The Master then had the drums beaten and ascended the seat first. A monk asked, "What is it like before the lion has emerged from its cave? The Master said, "Afraid."
A man saw his claws and fangs. He asked, "What is it like after leaving the cave? The Master said, "The head and tail cannot be hidden.
He asked further, "In that case, when there is spirit, one adds to the spirit; where there is no elegance, there is elegance nonetheless.
The Master said, "Beat the drum; everyone look! The Master then said, "Zhaozhou lived in this monastery for twenty years, yet his broken-legged meditation bench remains incomplete."
On one side, with ash on his head and dirt on his face, half-starved; the bitter family tradition has been passed down through ancient times and today.

One cannot help but laugh at the "elders" of the present day, who are just like officials inquiring about their office-fields (*zhítián*). "If the office-fields are plentiful, I shall go—so as to avoid the sight of my alms-bowl having nowhere to rest.
"If the office-fields are meager, I shall not go—I fear there will be neither salt nor vinegar. In the Chan school, such people are hard to find.
Good grandchildren! The True Eye has recently been like swept-away dust. Chief Seat Huilin has long kept his brilliance hidden;
within him, the fruit has ripened and naturally emits its fragrance. Casting for fish in the great ocean, one may win or lose; there is no harm in returning with an empty boat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Where all people know, Liang-sui knows completely; where Liang-sui knows, all people do not know. I wonder, what is it that Liang-sui knows?
The Master said, "A single character hangs from both ends. The monk stepped forward and said, "If one does not sleep on the same bed, how can one know the hole in the lining of the quilt?
The Master said, "To receive the words, one must understand the source. The Master then said, "One."
My almsbowl has traveled far, passing through several provinces; at crimson gates and humble thatched roofs, I sought [the Way] according to conditions.

Now, with feet blistered from walking, I have returned; I am free and easy as an ox at Mount Mui. If you understand it thus, it is still like a flower falling from oil—this is not yet the phrase for arriving home.
What is the phrase for arriving home? A single staff of sorrel leans against the corner of the wall; three nipples of dew...
The shoe rack was hung on the roof.
A fellow practitioner from Zifu Monastery held a Lotus Assembly to make offerings to the Arhats and invited the Master to ascend the seat. A monk asked:

"When the crimson sun emerges from the sea, its brilliance shines for ten thousand miles; when the precious mirror is set upon the stand, its radiance illuminates all directions. As a student who has come forward, I request—"

The Master said, "A single mirror. The Master said, "Faster than a sudden clap of thunder to cover one's ears. The student asked, "One phrase circulating, all people listen with bated breath. The Master said, "If a horse lacks the thousand-mile stride, it is in vain to pursue its wind-like speed. The student asked, "Who, hearing such a Dharma, would not resolve to attain Bodhicitta? The Master said, "What is Bodhicitta? The student asked, "The Southern School and the Northern Patriarchate are both like this; Heaven—" The Master said, "How can you say that? The student asked, "What is the meaning of 'Heaven'? The Master said, "It is the same as 'Earth'. The student asked, "What is the meaning of 'Earth'? The Master said, "It is the same as 'Heaven'. The student asked, "Why do you say they are the same? The Master said, "Because they are both without form. The student asked, "What is formlessness? The Master said, "It is the same as having form. The student asked, "What is having form? The Master said, "It is the same as formlessness. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no difference. The student asked, "What is non-difference? The Master said, "It is the same as difference. The student asked, "What is difference? The Master said, "It is the same as non-difference. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no distinction. The student asked, "What is non-distinction? The Master said, "It is the same as distinction. The student asked, "What is distinction? The Master said, "It is the same as non-distinction. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no separation. The student asked, "What is non-separation? The Master said, "It is the same as separation. The student asked, "What is separation? The Master said, "It is the same as non-separation. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no duality. The student asked, "What is non-duality? The Master said, "It is the same as duality. The student asked, "What is duality? The Master said, "It is the same as non-duality. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no coming or going. The student asked, "What is the absence of coming and going? The Master said, "It is the same as coming and going. The student asked, "What is coming and going? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of coming and going. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no birth or death. The student asked, "What is the absence of birth and death? The Master said, "It is the same as birth and death. The student asked, "What is birth and death? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of birth and death. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no self or other. The student asked, "What is the absence of self and other? The Master said, "It is the same as self and other. The student asked, "What is self and other? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of self and other. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no beginning or end. The student asked, "What is the absence of beginning and end? The Master said, "It is the same as beginning and end. The student asked, "What is beginning and end? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of beginning and end. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no past, present, or future. The student asked, "What is the absence of past, present, and future? The Master said, "It is the same as past, present, and future. The student asked, "What is past, present, and future? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of past, present, and future. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no samsara or nirvana. The student asked, "What is the absence of samsara and nirvana? The Master said, "It is the same as samsara and nirvana. The student asked, "What is samsara and nirvana? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of samsara and nirvana. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no delusion or enlightenment. The student asked, "What is the absence of delusion and enlightenment? The Master said, "It is the same as delusion and enlightenment. The student asked, "What is delusion and enlightenment? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of delusion and enlightenment. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no Buddha or sentient beings. The student asked, "What is the absence of Buddha and sentient beings? The Master said, "It is the same as Buddha and sentient beings. The student asked, "What is Buddha and sentient beings? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of Buddha and sentient beings. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no purity or defilement. The student asked, "What is the absence of purity and defilement? The Master said, "It is the same as purity and defilement. The student asked, "What is purity and defilement? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of purity and defilement. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no dharma or non-dharma. The student asked, "What is the absence of dharma and non-dharma? The Master said, "It is the same as dharma and non-dharma. The student asked, "What is dharma and non-dharma? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of dharma and non-dharma. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no truth or falsehood. The student asked, "What is the absence of truth and falsehood? The Master said, "It is the same as truth and falsehood. The student asked, "What is truth and falsehood? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of truth and falsehood. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no existence or non-existence. The student asked, "What is the absence of existence and non-existence? The Master said, "It is the same as existence and non-existence. The student asked, "What is existence and non-existence? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of existence and non-existence. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no light or darkness. The student asked, "What is the absence of light and darkness? The Master said, "It is the same as light and darkness. The student asked, "What is light and darkness? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of light and darkness. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no inside or outside. The student asked, "What is the absence of inside and outside? The Master said, "It is the same as inside and outside. The student asked, "What is inside and outside? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of inside and outside. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no center or periphery. The student asked, "What is the absence of center and periphery? The Master said, "It is the same as center and periphery. The student asked, "What is center and periphery? The Master said, "It is the same as the absence of center and periphery. The student asked, "How can there be sameness? The Master said, "Because there is no high or low. The student asked, "What is the absence of high and low? The Master said, "It is the same as high and low. The student asked, "What is high and low? The Master said, "It is the
The superior man asks further, "Who else is there? The Master says, "Today’s dialogue has some substance.
He continues, "Every word is clear and accords with the Way; at every door, one passes through Chang'an. The Master says, "Fortunately, you are pitiable.
Then he says, "Clapping hands as we meet, we laugh without end. Originally there is neither realization nor cultivation; everyone [possesses it] fully."

These are Arhats. Why must you seek them at Tiantai or Yandang? Do you understand? Amidst the shadows of fluttering banners and flowers, within the fragrance of blooming lotuses, every person has snow-white hair and frosty whiskers;
each one possesses the traces of clouds and the demeanor of a crane. There are even those who gaze intently at the cranes.
There were those who chanted sutras with their teeth bared; there were those who covered their heads with robes made of a hundred patches;
there were those whose long eyebrows shielded their eyes; there were those who tamed dragons and subdued tigers; and there were those who engaged in pure conversation face-to-face.

Although these various manifestations differed, they were all the playful display of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*). It was not seen that one day, while Master Yangshan was seated, an Arhat arrived, soaring through the air.
Yangshan asked, "Where have you recently come from? Luohan replied, "From India. Yangshan asked, "When did you leave there?
Luohan replied, "After the midday meal today. Yangshan said, "Why so late? Luohan replied, "I was traveling through the mountains and enjoying the scenery.

Yangshan said, "The playful exercise of supernatural powers is certainly not lacking in the Venerable One; however, as for the Buddha-dharma, it must be left to an old monk like me. Luohan [remained silent].

The monk said, "I have come specifically to the Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The Master replied, "This land has always had its own little Śākyamuni," whereupon the monk soared into the air and departed.
The Master said, "Old man Yangshan usually has eyes like rivers and a mouth like the sea, and his brilliance is swifter than a passing wind;
yet he was suddenly doused over the head with foul water and, in the end, did not even realize it. At that time, had he seen what I said—'This land has always had its own little Śākyamuni'—"
"Little Śākyamuni," he said, and pulled his staff to beat him out. "It is so; it is so. Yet, this blow might as well have been spared.
Why was it done thus? In these times of difficulty, one can only share the same incense and lamps; do not compare their strengths and weaknesses."
At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "I cite an instance from the past:
there was an old master who did not speak a single word to the monks for an entire summer. A monk sighed to himself, saying, 'I have passed this summer in vain like this;

I do not dare hope that the Master will preach the Buddha-Dharma, but even if I could hear two words of the True Cause, that would be enough. When the old master heard this, he said, 'Dharmācārya, do not speak such things so hastily. As for..."
"The true cause—there isn't even a single word. Having spoken thus, he tapped his teeth and said, "It was not appropriate to speak like that just now.
An old master living in a neighboring wall heard this and said, "What a fine pot of soup, ruined by two mouse droppings!
Xuedou said, "Whose kitchen pots do not have one or two [such things]? The Master said, "During the long summer, having no other diversion, I prepared a pot of soup."
The cauldron’s flavors are quite fragrant, yet the firm ground becomes stained with grime. The mouth is the gateway to calamity; the tongue is the axe that fells the body.
One has needlessly added three catties of iron, all because one gazed upon the rusted shackles. Suddenly, there is a monk who comes forth and says:
"The Master must also look after [his students]. Huilin simply said to him, "A dead mouse.
He ascended the hall and, citing Master Tongfeng, said: When a monk entered the gate, the Master raised his whisk; the monk then bowed.
Tongfeng said, "The dog barks at the moon. When another monk arrived, Tongfeng likewise raised his whisk;
the monk bowed, and Tongfeng struck him. When Master Shilou saw a monk enter, he raised his whisk;
the monk bowed, and Lou said, "So it is, so it is. When another monk entered, Lou raised his whisk; the monk bowed, and Lou struck him.
When Master Linji saw a monk enter, he raised his whisk; the monk bowed, and Linji struck him.
Another monk entered, and Linji again raised his whisk; the monk bowed, and Linji struck him as well. The Master said:
One person attains the samādhi of self-benefit; one person attains the samādhi of benefiting others; one person attains the samādhi of benefiting both self and others.
Let the person with clear vision examine and distinguish them.
Ascending the hall to thank the administrators: The small cloister of Hui-lin is just like a single boat; sailing upstream all day long, it must be pulled by many people.
Those who come and go come and go; those who speak of Chan speak of Chan; those who prepare the meals prepare the meals.

Strike the sleepy one, strike the sleepy one! Sometimes it is sweet as honey; sometimes it is bitter as gall. To deliver sentient beings in such a manner—this makes the Old Golden Immortal laugh to tears.
If you ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey, it causes people’s bellies to stew. Why does it cause their bellies to stew?
Because even when pressed by the ox-heads, they will not eat grass.
At Mount Jiuxian in Hongzhou, Elder Qin was invited to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages;
how then does a lineage master of the Dharma obtain it? The Master said, "It is when there is brightness within the darkness. The monk pressed further.
"If one does not transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, there will ultimately be no way to repay their kindness. The Master said, "That has already fallen into the secondary.
The monk asked, "Do you still permit this student to add further annotations? The Master said, "It is already more than enough.
The monk bowed and said, "A single moon rises over the sea; how many families ascend the tower? The Master then said, "Beside Tengwang Pavilion, far away..."
He beckons with his hand. Along the embankment of the Bian Canal, he does not yet nod his head. If you wish for the scaled fish to come onto the hook, everyone must row the wooden-orchid boat.
But tell me, how is the wooden-orchid boat rowed? After a long silence, he says: "Without disturbing the clear waves, the intent is naturally distinct."
The Master bestowed the Dharma robe. Holding it up, he showed it to the assembly and said: "To transmit the mind through the Dharma, and to manifest faith through the robe.
On the peak of Mount Huangmei, at the summit of White Lotus Peak, it is entrusted to one who travels the path of Caoxi. A golden seal cast from a single mold—why must this be necessary?
The Master smiled and said: "If one does not borrow the old lady’s skirt to tie it on, how could one dance wherever one goes?"
San Tai. That evening, he was invited by the Elder Jiuxian for a small discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said: "Today is the fifteenth day of the fourth month;
we already see the blazing heat of summer. It is only fitting to fan ourselves and drink water; how can one discuss the present or cite ancient precedents? Please, Elder Jiuxian..."

Old man! Pour forth some of that refreshing Dharma-rain. Among this assembly, those Zen practitioners with "nails for beaks" should step forward immediately and ask, until their mouths are as motionless as a foundation stone;
only then will you believe how difficult it is to be an Elder. Take care of yourself, Elder; to trigger the mechanism, one must use a crossbow of a thousand-jun strength.
As he saw off Elder Jiuxian, he ascended the hall and said: "In my declining years, Huelin has entered the red dust of the world; Bowing and rising for three years, I have grown weary at heart.
I laugh at myself, wishing to return home but unable to do so; From time to time, I see guests out at the capital city.

Therefore it is said: Worldly affairs are endless and weary; they are not as good as the mountain mounds. Green pines scatter the sunlight; azure ravines flow long and clear. Mountain clouds serve as a curtain; the night..."
The moon serves as a hook; lying beneath the wisteria vines, with a clod of earth for a pillow, eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty—there is truly nothing to do.
This is the free-and-easy water-buffalo of Mount Mui. Yet, although it is thus, if you simply proceed in this manner, what spirit is there in it?
The seven hollows and eight protrusions must be brought forth; do not rest until the six are molded into three.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Wearing black robes and guarding the black pillar, the tiger does not eat its own stripes; it fears harming its companion.
How is it that the worm within the lion’s body spends all day devouring the lion’s own blood? Enduring the pain, the golden-haired one makes no sound;

the flavor within this cannot be easily distinguished. From now on, bite and gnaw! I pray that when you turn your light back to reflect upon yourselves, you will finally believe that empty space has no [inherent nature]."
[On the subject of] divisive speech, he ascended the hall. He cited the ancient case where Master Guling asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From the city.
Guling said, "Do you know that your parents who gave birth to you are currently suffering in hell? The monk said, "I have come specifically to see this. Guling—
Linji asked, "How do you view this? The monk cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! Linji shouted, "What place is this? If you want to cry, then cry!
The monk said, "But what can be done about my parents suffering in hell? Linji asked, "How would you avoid this calamity?
The monk said, "Thirty years from now, there will be someone who recognizes the meaning of these words. The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "The Ancients..."
Master Ling was like one who causes people to fall on level ground or places thorns in soft mud.
If this monk had been a true master, as soon as he heard him say, "Do you know that the parents from whom you were born are currently suffering in hell? he would have immediately replied:
"If you wish to know the path through the parched sea, you must ask those who have traveled it. He would have waited for the old master to hesitate.
He then pushed over the meditation seat. Regarding the fact that today Liaochu, the attendant, performed memorial services for his parents, let me ask you all:
tell me, were his parents suffering in hell, or were they enjoying happiness among humans and devas?
If you are certain to attain it, I grant you one eye. If you are certain not to attain it, you will bring trouble upon your first attendant, who shall enter the boiling cauldrons and burning coals.
I, this mountain monk, shall recite for you a verse on "Breaking Hell," so that you may avoid making your living solely within the ghost cave.
Since your father and mother passed away more than twenty years ago, you have remained stuck there, unable to sever the ties.
This morning I broke open the antique chest; you invited me to ascend the hall to present a public case (*gong'an*). Guling stirred up wind and waves on level ground;
the dozing Chan practitioner can do nothing about it. Do not ask about hell or heaven; everyone simply partake of the roasted goose according to custom.
The donor has recovered from illness and invites the Master to ascend the hall, saying: "The Buddha’s illness and the Patriarchs’ illness are doubts within the minds of sentient beings.
If the dust of emotional attachments is shed in a single thought, they dissipate like the wind. Let us inquire into the source of all illnesses:
from what do their arising and ceasing depend? From where do they come? To where do they go? If one can see directly and immediately, there will not be a hair’s breadth of suffering. Not.
When Mañjuśrī went to inquire after the illness of the elder Vimalakīrti, they gathered their heads together to discuss medicinal prescriptions.
Why did he drive away the lion cub? He did not recognize the "leakage" of the Western Heaven; how many people have mistaken it for a crow's head?

Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival, a monk asked: "All grass is medicine; Mañjuśrī forcefully points it out. If one does not understand this, it causes people to engage in investigation by default.
As a student, I have come before you; I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip;
the sweet melon is sweet from stem to end. The monk stepped forward and said: "If that is so, then when we meet, there is no need to bring it forth; as soon as the intention is raised, it is known."
[The Master] said, "There is. As for that matter of 'knowing there is,' what is it? [The student] stepped forward and said, "How can one avoid it when entering a field of weeds?
One simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand. The Master said, "When will you emerge from this thicket of brambles?

[The student] said, "The *Mañjuśrī* koan is struck through with a single stroke. But as for the fact that the entire earth is medicine, which among them is the self? The Master said, "Step back, step back."
Later, a monk asked: "When Zhaozhou presents his wit within a phrase, the four gates face one another and he offers a light reply in vain.

The student does not yet understand the meaning herein; I beg the Master to use skillful means to point out its origin. The Master said: "Great, there is nothing outside it; small, there is nothing inside. The monk pressed further:
"If this is so, then at the moment of questioning one does not know the profound and subtle intent, while only upon answering does one see the mind of the Patriarch. The Master said: [Silence].
It is easy to emerge from within the gate; it is difficult for the body to exit through the gate. The student said, "How can one help it that no divergent views are sought within words?
The *śakara* eye is free from even a speck of dust. The Master said, "You have still not seen Zhaozhou.

The student said, "How many people follow along with words and chase after phrases, yet at every gate they say there are no obstructions? The Master said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its measuring basket."
The Master then said: "Today happens to be the Double Fifth Festival. There was a monk who asked about the circumstances of the occasion;
his question was indeed direct, yet he did not understand how to take it up within his own speech. For the sake of you all, I shall repeat it once more:
In the past, Mañjuśrī said to Sudhana, "Gather me some medicine. Bring back whatever is not medicine."
Sudhana entered the mountain and searched everywhere; there was nothing that was not medicine. Upon his return, he reported to Mañjuśrī, "In this mountain, there is nothing that is not medicine.
Mañjuśrī said, "Bring whatever is medicine here. Sudhana plucked a blade of grass and presented it to Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī received it and held it up, saying, "This medicine can kill a person, and it can also bring a person back to life. The Master said:
"A principle such as this is known only by those who have truly realized it. Unless one possesses eyes of iron and pupils of copper, one will often miss it right before one's face.
Nevertheless, although it is thus, when Sudhana gathered the medicine in that manner, he knew only one aspect; whereas Mañjuśrī’s discernment of the medicine in that manner..."
Knowing these two, he then picked up his whisk and said, "Do you recognize this medicine? Those who obtain it attain longevity; those who take it do not die.
Shen Nong did not know its name, and Jīvaka had no place to seek it. It eradicates the sicknesses of Buddhas and patriarchs and sweeps away ignorance and afflictions.
In every thing and at every point, nothing is concealed; the numinous light shines through—whom does it awaken?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the workings of Heaven there are wind, rain, darkness, and clarity; in human affairs there are good fortune, misfortune, regret, and prudence.
Favorable circumstances are few, while adversity is ever-present. This has been so since antiquity; why should one take it to heart? These are the discussions of worldly laypeople.
As for this old man of Mount Ling, past matters are like a dream and cannot be grasped; future matters are like a flash of lightning and cannot be anticipated."
Concentration. Present phenomena are like clouds, appearing as if they were there. By means of this expedient, one can perform what others cannot perform and endure what others cannot endure.
I, Huelin, shall provide an annotation for you all: past events are like dreams, clearly devoid of any gaps or seams.
You must take that which was done during a dream and employ it as if it were done while awake. As for future events...
Like lightning, its existence or non-existence cannot be seen. Do not let the mind of hope obscure your innate face.
Present phenomena are like clouds; they seem to exist before one’s eyes. How can one obtain a southeast wind to blow them away at the mouth of the western mountains? After a long silence, he said:
"I, this mountain monk, have blown it all to pieces for you. Do you understand? Do not say that being 'without mind' means there is 'no matter';
it has also caused King Xiang of Chu to grieve to death.
He ascended the hall and said: "To those coming from the south, I unload for them; to those coming from the north, I load for them. Zhaozhou and...
Even so he speaks thus; it is much like worldly sentiment observing the warmth or cold, and human righteousness adjusting to high or low.
Because of this one matter, I have gained one more wisdom: to those coming from the South, I give a smile; to those coming from the North, I give a smile.
In laughter there is no blade; in laughter there is no mystery. But tell me, what is the point? One need not worry that this matter will rot away;
though those who sell it are many, those who buy it are few. Elder Huelin’s eyes are fixed on a fool—dare anyone force an ox to eat grass?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Just now, the practitioner Qin led a young attendant carrying several lotus flowers.
Upon entering the gate, he prostrated himself. I, the mountain monk, asked him, 'What are you doing? The practitioner replied, 'I request the Master to ascend the hall and preach the Dharma.
I called for an attendant and had the lotus flowers divided into four vases and arranged there. The practitioner was at a loss. If you can realize this, what [further need is there]?"
I must now sound the Dharma drum and sit loftily upon the lion throne; the true eye of Vulture Peak has been transmitted all at once.
Since it is not otherwise, I cannot help but present this public case anew: first, to uproot the seeds of transgression and shatter the net of doubt for the Guo family;
second, to open a single eye for the practitioner. Have you not heard of the monk who asked Zhimen in the past about the lotus?
[The monk asked: "How is it when the flower has not yet emerged from the water? Zhimen said, "A lotus flower. [The monk asked: "How is it after it has emerged from the water?
Zhimen said, "A lotus leaf. The Master [Yunmen] said: "Zhimen was a master of the school; his utterances were like driving in a nail or cutting through iron.
Nevertheless, while this was so, he only knew how to hold fast, but did not know how to let go. Suppose someone were to ask me, 'What about the lotus flower?'"
How is it before emerging from the water? Smoke enshrouds the railings outside, where the green blades lean and sway. How is it after emerging from the water?
The wind shakes the stalks within the pond, each one fragrant. Ultimately, how is it? Thank you, O washerwoman, for not plucking them; you have left them in the rain to shelter the mandarin ducks.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Ten years I have served as abbot, yet this year there has been much clamor and strife. When one reflects on worldly affairs, even the Buddha cannot comprehend them.

Yesterday I purchased a divination chart and cast it; the reading says the coming year will be auspicious. The star of wealth and raiment shall enter my door, while the ghosts of depletion shall depart.
Let the administrators and heads each apply their own discernment. Prepare two cups of tea and offer them with great courtesy."
He smiled and said, "Let us all speak of joyful Zen, so that the staff shall not give rise to vexation.
On the birthday of the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva at Renwang Yuan in Kaibao, he ascended the seat for the third time.
As it was his final ascent, the Master looked over the assembly and, raising his right fist, said: "This very thing is the eighty-four thousand mudrās."
Luo Bi then raised his left hand and extended his five fingers, saying, "This is precisely the eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes.
He then smiled and said, "The Great Compassionate One descends at all times; the Buddhas appear without interval in every place.
Here, tear open the gateway of the face and realize the eyes and hands throughout your entire body. Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
A special messenger from Tianning Monastery in Yizhou invited the Elder Master to ascend the hall.
A monk asked, "What is Linji Chan? The Master said, "A wooden horse receives a severe lash. The monk pressed further, "What is Yunmen Chan?
The Master said, "An iron boat sails through space. The monk pressed further, "What is Caodong Chan? The Master said, "A perfect circle, missing half. The monk pressed further, "If..."
"What is the Chan of the Dharma-eye? The Master said, "A red brocade canopy over a flowered rug.

[The student] asked, "What is the Chan of Miao-yang? The Master said, "A golden needle threaded through the dark. [The student] asked, "I have received your instructions on the five houses and lineages;
as for the matter of the ultimate vehicle, what is it like? The Master said, "In every place there is water in the well; in whose hearth is there no smoke? [The student] asked, "As for a student..."
When a person comes here, they cannot understand the Master’s response to their question. The Master said, "I, too, cannot understand it.
The monk bowed; the Master said, "It is permissible to ask about matters. The Master then said, "The timing and conditions have their own inherent reasons."
Those who understand the music seek one another from a thousand li away. On the roads of Hanshan, a mere wave of the hand; by the banks of Shidi, a nod of the head has already been given.

The Governor of Yiyang has fortified the True Vehicle with walls and moats. He sent a formal letter from a thousand li away to seek you at the Imperial Court, mindful that the Chan gate has fallen into decline and striving to provide support for it.
Alas, he laments that the Way of the Patriarchs has become desolate, his heart resolved to protect it from without. Furthermore, Your Excellency...
The Elder is currently in the prime of his life and is in a hurry to benefit sentient beings;

he should simply take up his staff across his shoulder, lift his skirt, and seek to reopen an old shop, letting the people of the age come and go as they please for their buying and selling. There is no need for such humble persistence; I request that you simply accept the responsibility.
Even though it is thus, tell me: how do you express the single phrase for seizing the opportune moment? "The five-petaled flower blooms; spring fills the great earth.
The clay ox is spurred on to exert its spirit. Take well this melody from before the Hall of the Single Reed and offer it to those on the roads of the Eastern Lands."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "A hundred-year-old dark room can be pierced by a single lamp. What is this one lamp? The Master struck him.
The monk stepped forward and said, "What is the hundred-year-old dark room? The Master said, "You have run straight into a pillar.
The monk said, "In that case, the light penetrates everywhere. The Master said, "Do not pretend to be clever. The Master then said, "In the past, the Dharma..."
Once, while Fayan and Wukong were warming themselves by a fire, Fayan picked up the incense spoon and asked Wukong, "You must not call this an incense spoon.
I have already spoken; what do you say? Wukong replied, "Incense spoon. Fayan did not approve.
It was only after more than twenty days had passed that Wukong finally realized the meaning of this. Nowadays, when brothers [monks] are questioned, they immediately say, "It cannot be so."
Some call it "fire tongs. Others say, "The incense spoon is simply an incense spoon.
Still others pay no mind at all. Yet others say, "Master, do not deceive people. Others offer a turning word where there is no connection;
but if one deliberates in such a manner, what connection is there? When none of these apply, how then is it? After a long silence.
He said, "Do not be coarse-minded.
He ascended the hall and cited a four-line verse by Master Dushun, which has circulated through the monastic communities from ancient times to the present.

There have been countless interpretations and fabrications of it, simply because you have not passed the Patriarch’s barrier; thus, your path is strewn with many thorns, and you are immediately caught by others.
The throat is gripped fast; one cannot breathe out. For your sake, Huilin eliminates the disease of involvement, and further eliminates the disease of non-involvement.
"The ox in Huai state eats the grain"; one must understand the source when receiving the words. "The horse in Yi state has a bloated belly";
striking the south moves the north. One searches the world for a physician; at midnight, he releases the black hen. Moxibustion.
On the left shoulder of the Boar: ten times he knocked on vermilion gates, yet nine times they did not open.
He ascended the hall and said: "The rain has passed at dawn; the earth is free of dust. The greens are deep and the reds sparse—a profusion of spring.
The flower blooms upon the staff, yet people do not understand; in a moment of negligence, they obscure their original body. Formerly, a monk asked National Teacher Huizhong: "How is it..."
"This is the original body of Vairocana. The National Teacher said, "Bring me a pure water pitcher for the old monk.
When the monk took the pitcher and arrived, the National Teacher said, "Return it to its original place. The monk then asked again, "What is the original body of Vairocana?"
The National Teacher said, "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away. The Master said, "The radiance of the sun and moon does not fail to shine because of the blind;
the heat of summer and the cold of winter do not cease to occur because of those who resent them.
It is utterly bare and naked, with not even a thread’s breadth of place for concealment. Yet even this one does not understand—how much less could one cover it over? Return!
"Do you understand? After a long silence, he said: "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.
On another morning, as he ascended the hall, he said: "In spring sleep one does not know the dawn; when awakening comes, the sky is already bright. Before the seven-strip robe has even been put on—"

The five-flavored congee is fragrant first; the Chancellor rises at the crowing of the cock. While ordinary people are busy through the entire night, the Chan practitioner does not know how to report his service to the Sovereign.

Ascending the hall, he said: "On the path of Caoxi, do not concern yourselves with citing the ancients or debating the present. Before those with clear eyes, take care to avoid speaking of delusion or awakening.
You should simply put on your robes, eat your meals, and inquire after the Master; there is no further Chan or Way to be discussed."
There are those who strive through diligent practice to seek liberation; if you simply believe in this way, you will surely find lifelong joy and fulfillment.
Should you, however, hesitate or engage in deliberation, you cannot avoid falling into the ranks of the gradualist path. Why is this so? "The Lesser Vehicle speaks much of the Buddha;
the veteran general does not discuss war. Today is the birthday of Zhongyi Zhiguo; let us shift this gathering for wine and meat into a celebration of the Dharma.
Unfurling the bowl alone, he beats the drum of Yanguan; singing the song of Deshan, he serves the tea of Zhaozhou and fashions the cakes of Yunmen.
Arraying these illusory implements, he makes offerings to the shadowy and echo-like assembly of Chan practitioners.
With this meritless merit, he respectfully returns the gift of their arduous toil. Elder Huelin does not dare to embellish his words with one by one of these praises, fearing...

The Buddha-nature of all defiled persons is obscured. Why is this? All sentient beings recognize only the physical body composed of the four great elements produced by their parents; yet they do not know their original face prior to being born of their parents.
This is also called "the matter before the seven Buddhas," "the place where yin and yang do not reach," and "the primordial chaos."
Before differentiation, it is also called the period prior to the kalpa of emptiness, one’s own original self.

I recall a poem regarding an ancient person’s birthday, which I shall now present to the assembly. It says: "When I was not yet born, I existed in darkness, knowing nothing at all. The Lord of Heaven forced me to be born;
Having brought me into life, what was the purpose? Without clothes, he made me cold; Without food, he made me hungry. I return you, O Heaven!"
"You give me back. Return me to before I was born. These words are indeed excellent, yet they still lack the "aperture of a patch-robed monk" (the essential point of realization).
Today, I shall provide a commentary for you all: "When I was not yet born, the pillar was pregnant; it was dark and obscure, with nothing known.
What a lackluster fellow! Heaven’s Lord forcibly gave birth to me; from that moment on, it was simply you who held onto [this notion].

It is settled. Since I have already been born, what more is there for me to do? Why do you prattle on about others? Having no clothes leaves me cold; yet this very thing still exists. Having no food leaves me hungry;
yet there is naturally one who picks up the spoon and grasps the chopsticks. Return the heavens to the Lord of Heaven, and let me have my own self.
Try picking it out and showing it to me—return it to me as I was before birth. Say, what would that be?
Ascending the hall, he said: "During the day, people are preoccupied with worldly affairs; at night, they do nothing but sleep.
Forgetting to prepare for a discourse on Chan, I ask that you all do not hold me in blame. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "For nine years at Shaoshi, [Bodhidharma] uttered but a single phrase. Up until the present day, those in all quarters have been misled by its mention.
But tell me, which was that phrase he uttered back then? Is it 'Bring forth your mind, and I will place it for you'?"
"Is it not that which has already brought peace to your mind? Is it so? Is it not that which is vast and empty, where there are no sages?
Is it so? Do not mistake the horse-saddle bridge for your father’s chin. All the old monks of the world have gone astray in their explanations."
Today, this mountain monk shall provide a small measure of salvation for you all, so that the descendants of future generations need not each be left stumbling and faltering.
If you wish to raise [the essential point] without being deceived, each of you must turn the light inward and reflect upon yourselves.
Sitting alone at Shaolin for nine years, he was reduced to a state where his mouth was like a wooden beam. After a long silence, he said: "Even so, it has only been a deception."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Every thought-moment is eternally empty and still; its daily application possesses great power.

This is the place where the Buddhas of the three periods have practiced, the place where the six generations of patriarchs have practiced. It is the function of no-effort, yet this effort is not in vain.
Even so, you must still shatter empty space before you will succeed."
Ascending the hall, he raised the verse: "My mind is like the autumn moon; / A clear, bright pool in the green depths.
/ Nothing can be compared to it; / How am I to describe it? The Master said, "Hanshan could not say it—let us stop there for now. Can any of you say it?"
"You must have a mouth like a foundation stone before the light can finally leak through.
He ascended the hall and said: "A thousand ways of explaining, ten thousand kinds of metaphors—these only cause people to fail to awaken all the more.
Last night, the west wind revealed the celestial secret; the lush yellow chrysanthemums fill the road with fragrance."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Joyfully encountering this time of the birth of a Sage, there is nothing with which to repay the Enlightened Sovereign. We rely solely upon a single incense stick and strike the drum three more times.
Let us sing the Song of Great Peace together and walk the path that transcends the ordinary.

But tell me, how does one walk the path that transcends the ordinary? How does one sing the Song of Great Peace? After a long silence, he said: "I only wish that the sun and moon of Yao’s heaven may endure forever. He waited.
[The Master] saw the Yellow River clear ten thousand times.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the dharma of no-mind? The Master said, "A wooden man shakes flowers at midnight.
The monk pressed further, "What is the dharma of having mind? The Master said, "Horses gallop before the Fengle Pavilion. The Master then said:
An ancient said: "Sometimes a single shout is like the precious sword of the Vajra King; sometimes a single shout acts as a crouching lion;
sometimes a single shout serves as a probing rod or a blade of grass for casting a shadow; and sometimes a single shout does not function as a shout at all."
He then let out a shout. Now tell me: was this the Vajra King’s Precious Sword? Was it the Lion Crouching on the Ground?

Was it the Probing Pole and Shadow Grass? Or was it a shout used for no purpose at all? After a long silence, he said: "Falling flowers embroider the spring waters; the new moon combs the clouds at night."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I do not ask about the Patriarch’s intent coming from the West; what is the meaning of the single phrase regarding the opening of the furnace?
The Master said: "Holding fast to cold ashes deceives people. The monk pressed further: "In that case, one must surely burst forth like a glowing ember before one can see the old adept Danxia.
The Master said: "Save your eyebrows. The Master then said: "The north wind is like an arrow."
He shoots at the courtyard floor. Cold and desolate, the Chan gate has not a single thing. Thank you, all of you, for providing such warmth; you have diligently prepared the furnace for me.
To obtain a thousand taels of gold when one is wealthy is nothing extraordinary; it is only when one places a single ember in a cold spot that it is truly remarkable.
Only then do these aspects mutually complete one another. On the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one may spread out a net;
at the gateway of Buddha-activity, one can warm one’s hands. Within the midst of clamor and bustle, seeking is easy; within the depths of cold stillness, groping is most difficult.

It must be that withered wood gives birth once more to flowers, and even cold ashes flare up again with flame. Although it is thus, tell me: what is the single phrase that transcends time and oversteps the seasonal limits?
"How do you say it? After a long silence, he said: "In the end, the frosty night moon falls naturally into the front creek. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Since I came to Huelin, four times I have seen the 'Cloud-Recording' (the winter solstice) festival. I do not know how to craft a clever welcome;
how could I dare to be loquacious? If you are angry, then let you be angry; if I am clumsy, then let me be clumsy. If you wish to penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs, let go..."
Rest the mind-ground. If you do not rest it, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, everything will fail at once.
He ascended the hall and said: "For ten years I have held my fishing line upon the rivers and lakes; with my reed hat and straw raincoat, I remain just as I am.
Suddenly, the float on the tip of the pole moves; in a casual moment, I have caught a fish. He called to the assembly and asked: "Tell me, what is this?"
"The fish—do you still recognize it? Do not ask whether the tip of the pole is light or heavy; simply ensure that you do not return empty-handed from the river.

Having finished this narrative, the Master spoke again: "Huilin’s iron steamed bun has been made for many years. It is not that I have failed to bring it forth; rather, people themselves will not accept it.
To look at it makes one's teeth shiver with cold; to bite into it makes one's brow furrow. If it were not Zhang Pengju, who could [eat it]?"
No one dares to put their mouth to it. If you bite, go ahead and bite. But tell me, what flavor is it? After a long silence, he said:
"A clay ox carries the red sun on its back; a stone woman wears a jade ring upon her breast."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Caoshan, "I bring this raw jade to you, Master;
I beg you to polish it. Caoshan said, "I will not polish it. The monk asked, "Why will you not polish it? Caoshan said, "You must believe that Caoshan is a master craftsman.
The Master said, "Old man Caoshan let this monk down. Since he said he would not polish it, how can he speak of being a 'master craftsman'? Suppose someone were to ask me:"
Huilin, why do you not polish it? I simply tell him: "I only fear it is not jade; if it is jade, store it away for now.
Set it in a corner by the wall; in years to come, it will radiate its own light."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The true mandate of the Patriarchs is as impenetrable as water-tight seals. To accord with the conditions of sentient beings, one must fulfill the prescribed measure.
It is like casting gold to form a person: one observes only the person, not the gold. Their names are confusing; their forms are bewildering.
The reason for this is that all have lost the truth. Before our very eyes are the lanterns, the pillars, the pure jars, and the incense burners."

Windows, doors, and casements—all are but names and forms. Which one is the real? Do you understand this thoroughly? Only when the shoulder is strained does one know the weight of the firewood bundle;
only when the pool is deep does one realize the length of the fishing line.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wondrous secret of the Patriarchs is revealed at every turn. Yet sentient beings, in their daily activities, remain unaware;
they do nothing but stubbornly give rise to conceptual discrimination. Have you not seen how Lingyun encountered the peach blossoms on the road, and Zhaozhou pointed out the cypress in the courtyard?
How extraordinary! It is just like a single speck of snow upon a glowing furnace."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Even if a question and answer were like a lion’s somersault, or yielding and seizing like an elephant king’s trampling;
even if one were to indulge in the debate of a cascading river and exert the swift mechanism of a biting arrowhead—when viewed with the True Eye, there is not yet anything there.
Moreover, the Dharma is no different from the Dharma; the mind is this very mind. The ordinary and the sage share the same source; delusion and awakening are of one consistency."

Therefore it is said: "The realms of boundless lands do not separate self and other by even the tip of a hair; the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the beginning and end within this very thought-moment.
Thus, even a lantern and a pillar can transmit the mind; so too can a staff and a meditation seat.
From time to time it appears in the world; it is so in every atom, so in every thought-moment, and so in every land.
Long ago, a monk asked Master Changsha, "What is the preaching of the insentient? Changsha pointed to a pillar on the east side and said, "This one can preach.
The monk asked, "I do not know who is able to listen. Changsha pointed to a pillar on the west side and said, "This one can listen. The monk said—
"Did the Master hear it? The monk said, "If I had heard it, who would have brought up this story? The Master said, "The pillar on the east side speaks—does it have a mouth?
The pillar on the west side listens—does it have ears? A person of keen intelligence should grasp this immediately."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "It is said that when a Śrāvaka perceives the nature, it is like seeing the moon at night;
when a Bodhisattva perceives the nature, it is like seeing the sun by day. I wonder, how does the Master perceive the nature? Xuefeng struck him three times.
The monk then asked Yantou the same question, and Yantou slapped him three times. The Master said, "These two old fellows, as soon as they are questioned by someone, immediately raise their hands."
In a state of frantic confusion, suddenly someone asked the old monk, "How does the Master perceive one's nature?
The monk neither struck him with his palm nor hit him; he simply said to him, "Huilin’s forty-eight hairs—I am unwilling to pluck out even a single one.
His mouth speaks of compassion, yet when touched, he breaks into a rage. If you can understand this, you will not fail to be joyful."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a great city with four gates outside; those who come from various directions do not follow but a single path.
The Master then lowered one foot and struck the meditation seat several times with his whisk, saying:
"From which gate do you all enter? After a long silence, he said: "The front does not reach the village; the back does not reach the shop."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Watching the Lantern Festival at night, I slept until dawn. My paper quilt was as warm as spring; beneath it, I laughed 'he-he.
Now tell me, what was there to laugh about? When you were busy, I was sleeping."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an old case: A monk asked Caoshan, "Luzu faced the wall; what did that signify? Caoshan covered his ears with his hands.
The Master said, "The ancients were very much afraid that people would speak of it."
Ascending the hall to pray for rain, he said: "Cold Food Festival and Qingming have both passed; the wild peaches and red apricots have already withered.
For a long time we have not heard the rain from the eaves; it truly makes one miss Jingqing. At that moment, they all recited the name of the Dragon Sovereign Tathāgata Bodhisattva.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. Zhou Zihou of Zhenjiang has passed the examination. Why, then, can he not return? After a long silence, he said:
"At the head of the Yangtze River, the spring willows are green; they too must stir up a wind of sorrow for you. Zihou was about to take office when [the Master] passed away.

Born into hardship, his aspirations were set upon the azure clouds. Hardly had he passed the imperial examinations when he suddenly sank into the great night. To provide merit for his journey to the underworld, we perform these rites of veneration.

We pray that you, sir, may realize that birth and death are like dreams and illusions, and understand that the bonds of affection are like flowers in the sky. May you shed all mundane attachments and transcend to the other shore.
Do you all understand? One attains the highest degree amidst the flash of a stone-light; all is but a dream within the hollow of the Southern Branch.
There is no truth. That green robe and paulownia-wood headpiece are but trifles; how many people in Jambudvīpa have been deceived by them!
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example: One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The Master said, "A scorched brick strikes through the ice to its very bottom."

Ascending the hall at the commencement of the summer retreat, he said: "People from the four seas and five lakes, we share the same observance of the *dhūta* practice at Huilin Monastery. It is like learning to herd an ox:
body and mind must be thoroughly matured. Constantly plow your own field; do not trespass upon the grain of others. If even a single phrase is discordant," [the ox will stray].
What face do you have for these ninety days? Have you not heard it said: "The Way-man is the *udumbara* flower;

far, far away, the distant mountains are green"? He ascended the hall and said: "The myriad dharmas are the light of the mind; all conditions are but the awakening of the nature. If a patch-robed monk understands it thus, he is merely poking his head into the weeds.
Now tell me, what is the phrase for emerging from the weeds? How would you say it? "Since you have no mind, I too shall rest."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: There was once a monk living in a hermitage beside the Changsha Monastery who claimed he had met Nanquan.

Master Changsha Cen sent a monk to ask him, "How was it before you met Nanquan? The hermitage master remained silent, sitting firmly in his seat. The monk asked again, "What about after all? The hermitage master said, "It cannot be anything else.

When Changsha heard of this, he spoke a verse: Before meeting Nanquan, The whole body was a single ball of mud. After meeting Nanquan, The whole body is a single ball of mud. If you wish to know the difference between the two, Look at the dragon and the snake on the same branch.
The person sitting at the top of a hundred-foot pole—though they have gained entry, it is not yet the truth. One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole;
the ten directions of the world are one's entire body. A monk then asked, "How does one advance from the top of the hundred-foot pole?
Shishuang said, "Mountains of Langzhou, waters of Liuzhou. The monk said, "I ask the Master to speak plainly. Shishuang said, "The four seas and five lakes are the King."
[The Master] said, "In the midst of transformation. The Master said, "Cen the Tiger—if he had not spoken those subsequent words, he would still have been one who sits atop a hundred-foot pole.
He ascended the hall and said, "An ancient said: 'If you come forward and offer a greeting, ten thousand taels of gold will be consumed in a single day;
if you go down and say "take care," you will receive the offerings of the people of the four worlds. The Master said, "The ancients spoke thus; great indeed!"
It is like paying a high price for something; this causes students to invariably take it as a sign of something particularly sublime. Master Cishou said: "I have come up here to offer my greetings;
I am glad that your physical health is at ease. As I go down, I say 'take care. When autumn comes, there will be little accord with the cold water.
If you suddenly have a flash of realization here, do not say that Huelin has deceived you."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised up the words of Zen Master Dizang: "The family style of Dizang has no trace of substance;
with dust on his face and ashes on his head, he is cold and desolate. The Master said, "When the ancients spoke thus, it was like a black ox lying in dead water.
The family style of the Linji house has some trace of substance: as soon as one steps off the meditation seat, there is a great bustle. But tell me, what is this 'great bustle'?"
"Good. Cold and secluded, it is good. You love its sheep; I love its ritual. Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Entering the hall, he said: "Body and mind are as one; there is nothing beyond the body. To understand it in such a way is like climbing a tree to seek fish. Have you not heard it said:
'Like a donkey looking down a well'—how does that compare to 'the well looking at the donkey'?"
On the morning of the first day, he ascended the hall and said: "Coming in the cold, we share the same smokeless hearth; After the meal, we together brew snow-colored tea.
Satiated and sleeping soundly, with nothing to do— I know not how to repay the Sovereign."
The lay patron of Shouchun Prefecture invited the Master to ascend the seat at Tianqing Temple to distribute *han-xian* (sweat-shirts) to a thousand monks.
The Master said: "The trousers one was born with are entirely empty in their essence; Zhaozhou’s cotton robe has no seams or openings.

Beating the collar from the sleeve and cutting the lapel from beneath the arm, the seams and gaps are naturally difficult to find; truly, not even the point of a needle is revealed. Nevertheless, though it is so, let me speak."
Eating, one is never truly satisfied; wearing clothes, one merely avoids the cold.

How can these compare to this robe, which was offered by the donor Tuan Yue Duan Shisheng, flowing forth from a mind of pure clarity? At such a moment as this, how do you express it in a single phrase?
After a long silence, he said: "A single piece of faith, clear as water; The whole sky filled with harmony, warm as spring."
The Master spoke again in verse: "The gate of giving has opened not for just a single day; Though clouds and mountains lie a thousand miles away, how could one decline the toil?
If you wish to hear the melody of non-arising amidst the dust, First take up the sword of wisdom upon your seat.

The undershirt that clings to the flesh is easy to give away, But for those on the Way who possess a mind, it is difficult to digest. I pray your merit may resemble the Pagoda of Potaishan: One story completed, then another rises above it."

Layered Heights. Entering the hall, he said: "Intense heat and bitter cold follow one after another; at Huilin, I have seen the hearth-fire open four times. When a monk faces the fire, he knows the skillful means;
one must strictly avoid sitting in a circle guarding dead ashes. It is easy to do it this way, this way; it is not so easy to do it otherwise."
It is difficult indeed not to be thus; it must be that withered wood sprouts flowers once more, and cold ashes give rise to flames again.
