In the Chan gate, it is difficult to find worthy descendants; to seek meaning in every phrase is to lose the truth entirely.
The mountains are mountains and the waters are waters—do not struggle with intellectual interpretations to outdo one another in cleverness.
Through various restings in non-mindfulness, one is naturally at ease among the pines and upon the rocks. There is no need to dispute the boundaries of fields and gardens;
the entire great earth is but a single finger-tip.
Do not laugh at the mountain monk’s coarse words; where can true reality be found through effort? Worldly people exhaust their spirits in search of it;
how could they ever find a fish by climbing a tree?
At the Qinghui Hall by the old master Quanyuan of Yaofeng:

The deep, clear lake reflects the brilliance of the moon; The sound of fishermen’s songs fades as the morning breeze clears. Clad in tattered robes, he sits in the full-lotus posture upon Mount Mengding.
Seated, he does not speak of poetic sentiment, but speaks of the Way.
The emerald pool is deep and still, containing autumn like a broad mirror; its clear sweetness is sipped at will, chilling the teeth. Lingyan laughs at himself for this desolate mountain.
Bones. The Moonlight Spring is stingy and wishes only to dry up;
at Duojing Rock, I shall hang my six rings upon the azure vines. All manner of fine sights before me belong to this secluded stillness; with my two eyes washed clean, I gaze until nothing remains.
Tired of it, he blocked the head of the well with *chátóu* grass in a single room.
In the Baoyun Well, Baoyun cleared the weeds and expanded the Chan grove; he excavated the stone to reach its source, his intent being profound. He sighed deeply that the Ganshui Well was not worthy.
The road stretches on; vast and boundless, it vainly seeks to aid the hearts of men.
The ancient cave of White Dragon is deep and profound, none dare to peer within. Dense and dark are the trees and grasses as wild clouds drift by. Where does the White Dragon submerge its head?
The world’s blue-haired commoners look to you for their return. At Guanyin Rock, he smiles at the sun;
wild flowers bloom beneath the green ridges. He sings of spring among the secluded birds amidst the white clouds. Here lies the entire body of the Great Being of Potalaka.
Dew. It brings vexation to the traveler who gazes at the mountains in vain.
From beneath Mount Sumeru, one looks down upon all other peaks as mere offshoots; its solitary loftiness rivals the lunar disc itself. Sudhana, there is no need to seek another peak.
Seek! At this very moment of rest, you shall see De-yun.

Beneath the pine gate, the cold, parasol-shaped pines stand like an unfurled canopy. They beckon noble guests; their eyes are doubly green. The old man of the Abbot’s Quarter welcomes and sees them off.
It is still early; you should not yet descend to the deep courtyard because of me.

In the eastern study, let the meditation board and rush mat pass the long days; by the bright window and clean desk, reflect upon the sparse bamboo. As one incense burner burns through the six periods of the day...
I have passed through [the world], and increasingly I perceive that the flavor of the Mountain School (Shan-jia) is truly authentic.

At West Hermitage, I concealed my form, long resenting that the mountains were not deep enough; I closed my door so that the dust of the mundane world could not intrude. Now, however, affairs rush before my very eyes.
I depart. To whom could I speak of this mind?
I have built a thatched hut on the Western Mountain; all day long there is nothing to do.

Thus, I have composed the "Twelve Verses on Lake Dongting" to reveal the Way that sentient beings fail to recognize in their daily lives. Zhaozhou said: "People of the time are bound by the twelve..."
At that time, the messenger said, "The old monk has mastered the twelve periods of the day. These words were most poignant, yet no one understood them.

At the hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.), when the cock crows, a single cry awakens the elder in his hermitage. He puts on his robes and treads upon the moonlight to listen to the pines and the wind; regarding the myriad affairs of the human world, he is too weary to open his mouth.

At dawn, at the hour of Yin (5–7 a.m.): Layer upon layer of lakes and mountains, true to the eye before one. If you further seek to discuss the profound and subtle within this, the seventy-two peaks will surely laugh at you.

At sunrise, at the hour of Mao (7–9 a.m.): In practicing Zen, one must strictly avoid artificiality and cleverness. Lately, monks have been studying empty gestures; they have never yet tasted [the truth].
When the rice is first served, one says "I am full.
At the hour of eating, whether the gruel and rice be fine or coarse, they nourish this sick body. The eggplants and bitter herbs are abundant this year;
who will think of the person emaciated within the hermitage?
At the hour of Yuzhong (Yi), the woodcutter comes to speak of human affairs: "On the riverbanks in the sixth month, the soldiers have not yet ceased;
all these things arise from the hearts of sentient beings.

At noon, the sun is at its zenith: the tile brazier and stone cauldron are but idle household items; gathering firewood and blowing on the flame, he brews tea for himself, smiling as he shares it with his child.
Childish and familiar in manner, before the sun has turned its course, he rises abruptly and sweeps the ground with his skirt. The hermitage is desolate and no guests arrive;
why does the yellow dog in front of the gate bark?
The hour of *bùshí* (the seventh watch). I laugh at myself that my indolence throughout my life has been genuine; with white hair and a weathered face, I have spent little time in service.

Let them be joyful, let them be angry. The hour of *rùyǒu* (the eighth watch). Within the realm of light, how could anything endure for long? There is no more Buddha-dharma to deliberate upon; listen to this patch-robed monk.
The child runs about crosswise.
At dusk, the hour of Xu. What does it matter that there is a mouth? It hangs long upon the wall. Half the autumn colors are rolled up by the western wind.
A single point of green lamp-light illuminates the thatched room.

The hour of Ren-ding (Hai): Dwelling in the mountains, one maintains the ancestral style; growing old, one finally attains the leisure to sleep with an open mind. In human life, do not let yourself be hindered by idle fame. The hour of Ye-ban (Zi):
With a paper curtain and a pine bed, sleep is truly beautiful; turning over, one does not even realize the toil of this life—how many are there who do not?
Driven by the impulses of mind and consciousness, I arrived at Ke-tang on West Lake in Hangzhou seeking seclusion from clamor;
yet the lake and mountains would not let me rest. Treading through worn-out straw sandals, my wandering remains unfinished.
I have wandered everywhere, and now willingly cast my lot among the two mountains in old age.
I rejoice to see that your heart remains steadfast through the years. Shutting my door all day long, I face the jade-like bamboo;
had we met without the eyes of Xiangyan, we would have seen nothing but the wind beating and the rain falling.
Inscription on Crossing the Cold to Reach Tiantai at Stone Bridge I did not come for the green waters and blue mountains; I am ashamed that I lack the strength of legs to cross the bridge.

Yet I rejoice that there is a tea cup to serve the Sage. From the azure cliffs, the waterfall pours like the broad Milky Way; As the clouds dissolve over Fangguang Peak, the golden light shines forth.
The Hall opens. I inquire after the venerable elder with the thick eyebrows; he too must turn his head back to enter the dust of the world.
[This is] inscribed by Bai Daoyou:

"Fierce tigers and venomous snakes follow the transformation of the Dharma; malevolent spirits and a hundred monsters look up to the lofty traces. It is all because of a single thought that divides the mundane from the sacred."
Saint, you block the path ahead at Zhengbing Peak.
At Lücheng Jiedai Monastery, I have come to briefly unpack my bundle; exhausted, I rest upon this long bed. I entreat you, Elder Wood: do not trouble yourself with such excessive chatter.
This single body is like a common inn; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. Exert yourselves, you travelers of water and clouds; you should seek out those who have realized the Way.
Upon first arriving at Mount Bao, there was a heavy snowfall.

I playfully inscribed these lines: Last night I stayed overnight on Mount Bao; In my thatched cottage, the green lamp glows and the hearth is full of fire. I imagine the mountain deity must be pleased in his heart.
I have awakened; the snow on the crag trees is blurred at dawn.
The next day, there was a magpie nesting in a jujube tree in front of the hermitage. The tree was several feet high. Thus, I playfully inscribed this verse.

The magpie’s nest is low in the tree, utterly free from alarm or suspicion; one may verify that the hermit-monk’s mind has long since turned to ash. Let us pass our days in the forest with our mouths sealed;
there is no need for empty joy in reporting that someone has arrived.
Planting pines, planting pines—one must seek out the crooked pine for planting. Once nurtured, it becomes a gnarled timber of the mountain forests; truly, there is no one to cast a glance upon it.
Only in the cold of winter does it find its place leaning against the ancient crags.
I planted a small pine with my own hands;
now a foot tall, it already reaches toward the clouds. It refuses to emulate the fragrant blossoms of the peach and plum in spring.
I imagine that by the day its dragon scales reach a girth of several armspan, this old monk will surely have been reborn.
Inscription for the Yi-xiao Hermitage:
I have quickly bound thatch to shelter against wind and rain; The earthen bed and rush mats are naturally dignified. Prosperity and decay passing before one’s eyes are but human affairs;
I entrust them all to the mountain monk’s single laugh.
In old age, one perceives the physical frame gradually decaying; with a liberated mind, all day long my eyes are like furrows.
Though I fear that my reputation for idleness may spread, I am still glad that returning to my hermitage was not too late.
Inscription for the Yuhou Hermitage:
A hermitage made of crooked wood, a bed fashioned from earth; The door stands open, yet there is no hindrance. Let not the people of this age laugh at the simplicity of my household style;
When the mind finds rest, all things are forgotten.
Singing on the upper floor, her words were elegant and refined. "Since you have no heart for me, I shall let it rest. She struck upon the matter in my lord's heart:
our former love has grown cold and desolate.
Waking from sleep, I playfully inscribe these lines:
Passing the time eating porridge and rice, Listening to the wind and listening to the rain while sleeping. Do not easily transmit this Dharma of peace and bliss To others.
Inscribed on the occasion of the Cold Food Festival flowers.
Countless flowers at the Cold Food Festival; in their silent solitude, they share the same state as the weeds. Only because their colors have faded do they remain here, aged within the mountains.

Their youthful splendor is rarely appreciated by men, and without fragrance, the butterflies do not know them. The human heart still favors reds and purples, vying to gaze upon the drunken West River beauty.
Inscription on the Newly Made Paper Robe: Wearing this paper robe in Pengheng, what harm is there in walking through the snow with arms flung free?
Since I neither pity others nor seek their love, from now on the world shall be spared its strife.
When the Master first arrived at Baoshan, he saw a small pond, as clear and lustrous as ice or jade. An elderly man said, "In the past, there was a white tortoise in this pond;
it has already been offered up. Thereupon, the Master named it Baiguiquan (White Tortoise Spring).

Even during times when the flowing gold melts the stones [of summer], this spring remains limpid and deep, filling the secluded pool. Having heard of this, the White Tortoise presented itself to Heaven.
My son, why do you limp about in the mud? When the spring is hidden, its water remains sweet and inexhaustible;
when people are at leisure, the Way becomes even loftier. A gentle trickle is sufficient for its own purity; do not toil to create waves and billows.
The Bao Mountain well was excavated;
the mountain bone was hewn to a depth of sixty feet. Within the rock, the spring eye finally opened. Those who drink the water later know its source;
it was once the labor of the mountain monk’s mind and strength that brought it forth.
The junior disciple carries bricks to build a stupa, stooping his back as he bears them up the mountain peak; wishing to complete a small tower rising amidst clouds and mist.
Gathering sand is like the play of children, yet for now, let us form a slight affinity with these lakes and mountains.
Entering meditative absorption, Avalokiteśvara-Nāga is always in samādhi; there is never a time when he is not in samādhi. For the sake of those who are distracted, he manifests such signs.
Master Guangruiyan called out, "Master of the House! and [the Master] responded, "Yes."
The protagonist, Nuo, listen to my words: the cycle of birth and death flows on without ceasing. Busy today, busy tomorrow;
when will this single point of numinous light be realized?
Listen to my words, O protagonist: when will the pursuit of fame and profit ever end?
How much better it is to recognize your own precious treasure—the numinous light, brilliantly radiant and boundless.
The protagonist Nuo listened to my advice: "In this fleeting life, do not be a man of deceit.
Though you may manage to deceive others in secret, in the light of day, it will inevitably dissipate."
Listen to me, O protagonist: a hundred years pass like a flash of lightning; at forty-five or fifty, one looks back no more.
I ask you, when do you intend to wait for?
My protagonist Nuo has heeded my instructions; this year he is already fifty-six. As a man, he has always been somewhat lacking in discernment.
On what day shall there grow white mold upon his lips?

I urge you: rather than eating meat, how would it be to chew on vegetable roots? Strive instead to let the fragrance of the precepts permeate your body and mouth. Do not say that there is no cause and effect after death;
for every eight *liang* one receives, one must repay with half a *jin*.
I urge you to eat only vegetarian food at dawn and morning;

though you may not yet be able to abruptly sever meat and wine, you should at least cultivate the causes of purity at these times. This saves expense and reduces karmic conditions while simultaneously preserving merit.
Lingyan’s words here are truly generous toward others.

Since our parting at the Reeds River, Master Huaijingzhao, the shadows of wild geese have vanished among the thousand peaks. Only upon hearing that the Emperor’s decree has been returned do we truly perceive the mind of the Master.
Your years in the chamber of calculation must now be nearly complete; the Zen gate grows ever more profound. When autumn comes to the summit of Mount Ou, I often again dream of the needle being cast.

Reading the *Recorded Sayings* of Chan Master Fojian, his discourse on Chan seems like that of an old man of Zhongshan: "Having a mouth but no mind—who knows? I demand thunderbolts from the tip of his tongue;
I apply the tongs and hammer within his own eyes. In ordinary times he draws the sword that brings life; in perilous moments he serves as a bridge for the dead."
The horse-doctor: "The master of the Zen forest remains; he has swept away the doubts of a hundred lifetimes for others.
He requests to retire from Huilin Temple, leaving his foot tied to an old ox with a single thread by Master Fuguo.
His heart wishes to go east or west, yet it is not yet free. We rely upon the eastern wind to pull him back together."
Power! He was sent early as a boatman to Yangzhou to pay his respects to Master Yi of Shouchun, who heard that he had taken up the handle of Dongchan’s wooden ladle.
"Open the sack and let it flow forth; this shall be transmitted to future generations. Later people will find their own worthiness lacking when compared to these words.
Practice! A wall-like family style must be resolute and decisive.
In response to National Teacher Noh:
"In old age, I sleep much more than a spring silkworm; atop the mountain of the five aggregates, I have pitched a hut. I eat when hungry and drink when thirsty, according to my lot."
[The Master] said, "Pass on. I do not know where you will encounter your fellow student.

I have heard from Master Shao of Dongchan that you are currently sitting at the head of the assembly at Tiantong. Deeply probe and strike with painful precision; you must not stop. In our school, there is directness—no nesting place."
Mortar and Pestle. Only when the house is broken and the people gone does one begin to have freedom. Master Guangdeng replied:

"Having retired from Cui Feng, there are scriptures to shield my eyes; by the bright window, no affairs disturb my heart, and the white days are long. I gather pine branches myself to burn as incense."
Alms bowl. Watching people all day long, their heads bustling in competition.
The gate of the monk and practitioner Qingxian Gui is as cold as autumn colors; throughout the entire day, no worldly carriage ever comes. Lately, he has become addicted to his passion for poetry.
Excellent. An old monkey wails in the cold window at night.
Sent on Mid-Autumn to Master Gui:
The lofty peaks and high ridges are but a few inches away; Green pines always accompany white clouds in their leisure. Enjoying the Mid-Autumn moon together over Lake Dongting.
The Moon. Who says that those of the mountain home do not come and go?
Reverend Hegui, as he grows old, his mind has become as soft as mud; he has divined Xu Lake to serve as his Tiger Creek. Amidst the misty waves of the seventy-two peaks—
How vast! Listen to this wanderer whose path has become lost.

Last year, I was able to find you at West Valley; through snow-covered bamboo and frost-bitten pines, the single path was deep. In the round hut, by the blue lamp, I heard your wondrous words, which caused the worldly heart of my entire life to be extinguished into ashes.
I need only to have my spring sleep fulfilled beneath a thatched eave; why must I compare the tally of years spent in a stone chamber?
I know from afar that since our parting you have been full of leisurely ease, sitting and listening as the pine wind clears ten thousand valleys.
The demon army of reflected images fills my eyes; like drifting clouds, worldly affairs—hurry to withdraw your head. Leaning on a rush mat, I sit in dullness, too weary to open my mouth.
Can you, O Poetry Debt, grant me a reprieve?
Master Hexin’s person drifts like a tumbleweed from one place to another; a hundred years of life pass between the crossing of arms. By what means did this stone bridge become a chance encounter?
Amidst the shadows of war and smoke, one finds a moment of leisure.
I rejoice that the ice-pitcher within your breast is pure; only I understand how you are rich in the Way yet poor in body. The fire of profit and the boiling cauldron of fame are at a seething boil;
all day long, people watch as they scramble their hands to grasp them.
Shown to Venerable Gaowei, and also addressed to Master Baohua Jian: The dream of three lifetimes atop the Stone has long since ceased to be;
Among the myriad affairs of the human world, eyes are but like eyebrows. Returning home, ask the old man of Baohua once more:
How does this compare to when you sat upright upon the meditation platform?
The eminent figure of Senior Seat Huìyuán has not betrayed his promise of those years; I recall him now, suddenly commanding my carriage to come. Let worldly flavors be as sweet as honey as they may;
the mind for the Way shall ultimately remain cold as ash. My thatched cottage is but a small three-bay dwelling; this stone couch is for you alone.
He smiled and opened [his mouth]. Leaning on his staff in the spring breeze, he spoke of the past. He sent word to the monkeys and birds: "Do not be startled or suspicious.

I, Huiji, encountered that venerable monk in my later years; we joyfully met. He cleared away the weeds and made a pact with me to grow old by the river's edge. Worldly sounds and emptiness have turned over many times.

Secluded within the forest, his circle of associates knew neither old nor new. For years his scholarly efforts had occupied the lecture hall; now, with a single sweep of true spirit, he has cleansed all emotional dust.
Lately, the hundred birds have no place to seek him out; the mountain flowers bloom everywhere in a profusion of spring.

To show this to those devoted solely to Chan: Since I departed from my old garden, much time has passed; seeing you, my son, I can still slightly raise my brows. Hearing your local dialect each time, I am moved to a faint smile;

as for the feelings of a traveler, there is no longer cause for further sorrow. In seeking your teacher, be careful not to be greedy for sleep or food; stand in the snow until you have finally attained thorough penetration.
The marrow and the skin—these are ultimately external to the Chan school; words such as "zhi," "hu," and "zhe" need not be known.

To show that a discerning Chan practitioner seeks a teacher and inquires after the Way is no mere trifle. Do not be like a fool who sleeps until satiated; the sun is already sinking in the west like a speeding arrow.
Sighs. A rosy countenance fades away as if led by a rope. With severed arm, standing in the snow, I contemplate my ancestors; piercing my thigh and hanging my head, I emulate the sages of old.
These words must be treasured and remembered; do not let the passing years slip by in negligence.
To the Chan practitioner Tan: A few thatched huts by the sea gate; a life of clouds and water, simply following conditions. With weary feet, one is too lazy to groom a horse for the road;
with fragrant incense, one plants the lotuses of Master Yuan. What would ten thousand measures of worldly salary avail? How could it compare to a single [moment] among the forest trees?
Awaken from sleep. On another day, he will surely come to fulfill his promise; for you, I shall show how a mustard seed can contain the three thousand worlds.

To those who seek Chan, I demonstrate that the single point of numinous light is inherently clear, piercing through the sentient beings' emotions of compliance and resistance. Pressing forward to see, the entire body opens into the Right.
Only with the eyes can one strike three o'clock at midday.

To the Chan practitioner Xiang, I show that once the ancients attained [enlightenment], they simply rested; in their thatched huts with green lamps, they sought nothing at all, merely using yellow scrolls to cover their eyes.
Unfolding it: where there is no elegance, he manifests elegance.
He shows the Chan practitioner how to set down the thousand-pound burden and return once more to the old three-rafters in the mountain valleys; there is no need to toil in search of Yangzhou.
Cranes, keep me company as I sleep upon my skeletal bones amidst the forest trees.

To the Chan practitioner Jiao, I show that worldly affairs are not worth turning one's head to look back upon. On another day, the lakes and mountains shall come for me; clad in grass garments and eating of wood-fruits, we shall be companions.
[Verse: Passing by, who would deign to open their thatched gate at random?
Seng Daocheng resided at Jinsan (Golden Mountain). He lived in a single dilapidated room and maintained the vow never to descend the mountain.
[The Master] admired his solitary purity and presented him with this verse:
When the mind comes to rest, demons naturally diminish; sitting alone on a mountain peak, one nurtures harmony with Heaven. Do not begrudge the narrowness of a thatched hut;
for as soon as the hut becomes spacious, affairs multiply.
Master Anzheng sought a verse:

"The yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying were known as such long ago; the tiles used to knock at the door shall likewise be left behind. Once one has lectured upon the True Sutra within the void, one will understand the laughter of the stone that nodded its head in years past."
The bright pearl at the bottom of the robe, sought by the Head Seat, is fundamentally perfect and round. Within this, there is neither right nor partiality.
Sitting all day on a rush mat and a paper screen, one should realize the bitter-mouthed Chan of the former master.

The one who reaches dhyāna seeks verses as a probing pole or a blade of grass to test the shadows; alone he plays and single-handedly wields the broken bamboo sieve. With lips parched and mind extinguished, all outflows are exhausted;
the rhombus-shaped mirror shines with its own brilliance without being wiped.
Sweep away jade verses and golden sayings; if you do not value your own numinous spirit, what can you seek from the sages?
In the place where the ghost of impermanence finds it difficult to swallow you, it is simply because you have attained freedom.
Daozhi changed his clothes and went to study under him.
He sought a verse but did not see it; Xukong understood the lecturing on the sutras. Within this, one must strictly avoid calculating progress by stages.
If the seven蒲團 (būtún) have been sat upon without being worn through, how can one casually clarify the nature of life and death?
All wondrous phrases and profound words are brought to rest; simply look at this single ox in the open field.
Suddenly, when the sharp rope from its nostrils snaps, it roars at the moon and plows through the clouds, becoming truly free.
Attendant Kang sent his junior disciple Siwen to Bao Mountain with a letter. Wen requested a verse separately, and I also showed him this one for Master Kang:
A light leaf-boat floats upon Lake Tai; From the Western Mountains he comes seeking an old monk’s dwelling. When you return home, you should strive to cultivate life-giving virtue.
It is said: "Peaceful at the foot of the forest is the level path.
Master Fazhao requested a verse:
An old cow with horns and a hairy hide, Tugging at the plow and pulling the harrow through many autumns— The heels of her feet never follow after others.
Turning. His nostrils pierce the heavens and he attains freedom. Having attained freedom, he is coldly silent amidst Lake Dongting.
I, the old monk Huíyīn, have sung my fill of the robe and bowl; wishing to cast off this body for cremation, I leave these two verses as a warning:
"The robe and bowl, in my old age, I have sung away entirely. Bare and naked, the body is even more at ease. One need only ensure that what was born of one's mother remains."
Wearing trousers, one does not feel the cold even when struck by snow or buffeted by wind.
What is the use of seeking a "good death"? It is better to endure a "bad life. Following conditions and according to one's lot, one dwells by the side of a rocky crag.
Even after being scorched by a wild fire, the spring breeze will still blow one back forth as before.
Because the practitioner of Chan wished to compile a record of his words, I stopped him with this verse:
"When our Patriarch first arrived, there were no written characters; later generations of disciples vied with one another to compile books.
My son, do not now labor over writing; keep secret the bright, perfect pearl atop your head."
Anzhen was the special envoy of King Siguang to invite [the Master]. He traveled a great distance to Guoqing Temple, but [Hanshan] declined him with a verse:
"Fenggan is truly a garrulous fellow; he has drawn upon himself the specific visit of Liuqiu. This will repeatedly bring trouble to Hanshan and Wuxue."
At this place, the gate of the crag should not be opened from now on.
When Grand Master Dàkōng was about to shave his hair, [Zhaozhou] stopped him with a verse:
"If you can turn things, you are a Tathāgata; the true eye opens upon a heap of refuse. This follows along with the inverted views of sentient beings.
The Dharma is willing to bestow a single point to cleanse the spirit-mirror;
whether in accord with or contrary to conditions, all is Chan. Remaining at home does not obstruct the conditions for leaving it behind. Master Pang and his son sit together in a circle;
only then is it realized that the discourse on non-arising is not partial.
Huilin: Admonishing the Zen practitioners upon entering the bathhouse:
when bathing, use but a small ladle of hot water; by making such frugal use, one’s days in this floating world will be long.
Though the value of sandalwood and cinnamon has not yet been spoken of in the capital, how many men must toil at the hundred-foot well?
Admonishing my disciples: It is not by mere coincidence that we share this single boat upon the waters; there is a profound karmic affinity for us to rely on one another as a community.
However, as I dwell in the mountains, wherever I may be, I shall never allow my monastics to sleep while still wearing their robes.
Entrusting my head seat Sui with my final years on the Western Mountain, I shall do nothing at all; in this place where I grasp a thatched hut, I can dwell in secluded seclusion.
Of the thirty-six thousand acres of Lake Tai, Heaven has granted them to this mountain monk as his Tiger Brook.
Sent to Elder Kuang of Guoqing Temple, also to be shown to the various monastics:
"The long discourse on the bitter-mouthed Chan of Han and Shi has gone unapprehended for many years; now we shall turn the family style back around.
You must vigorously apply the whip to the clay ox."
Fenggan’s leaking was due to his loquaciousness; he sketched out empty space, and it was all him.
Turning to laugh at Lüqiū for having no nostrils, he prostrated before the stove to seek Mañjuśrī.
Gathered heads forming a sign—do not ask at all. How can that matter be brought forth? When the belly is relaxed, the ocean is vast;
there is nothing in the world it does not contain.
The Elder Huishi Sheng sent this from Wan-sui, far away from Tenzhi. You should know that I am old and decrepit;
standing supported by others on the water’s edge or atop stones, I open the True Eye for you, my son, from time to time.

Having requested the site of the ancient Bao Shan Temple from the Abbot of Shixiang Monastery, I have made my secluded dwelling among bamboo windows, pines, and cypresses. When shall I come to visit you with a single boat,
to exhaustively discuss how all matters in the human world are ultimately false?

As the Chan practitioner Songju returns home to visit his kin, the mist and waters stretch boundlessly before him. His true nature is revealed by the golden autumn wind as the tree leaves turn yellow;
yet regarding that single phrase from before one’s parents were born, one knows not where one’s true hometown lies.
Sending off Chan Master Zheng on his return home:
To raise a stupa for his original teacher, though the master’s bones have long been cold; from a thousand miles away, he has come back specifically for this.
If you wish to understand that coming and going are uninterrupted, within this very state not a single step has ever been moved.

Seeing off the Chan practitioner Xian as he departs the capital to return to the mountains is truly a superior excursion. For a man of the Way who has traversed the world, there is fundamentally nothing to seek. His small boat heads east, light as a leaf;
looking back at the red dust of the mundane world, he lets out a smile and leaves it behind.
Seeing Master Zhen off as he gazes at his son’s returning boat by the lake: At the foot of the forest, one is first startled by the autumn of a single leaf.
One must be like a wild goat whose horns hang long out of reach; Do not let the hunting dog discover its tracks.
Sent to Chan Master Quan: On behalf of the Elder Puhui Sheng as a special messenger, I send this letter back to the lone peak before the spring blossoms.
To transmit these tidings, how could I decline the toil? Return home and seek out the axe for dwelling in the mountains;
become one who transcends the common in the monastic grove.

The Chan practitioner who delivers the seal [of realization] must be like a block of jade deeply concealing its potential; do not be like a needle in a bag, exposing its point. At every place, close the gate and sit in peace;
it does not hinder one to keep the mouth as still as a pair of tongs all day long.

Seeing Elder Guangfachu descend to the countryside, leaning against crags and beside waters, I am content to grow old. When you lower your hands to enter the hall at the proper time, we shall return on another day to share porridge and rice;
there will be no need to trouble anyone to carry the broken cauldron.
I visited the abbot of Fabao Hermitage, but the practitioner had gone out of the mountains with the clouds.
The windows and eaves possess a fine aesthetic; the pines and bamboos preach the Dharma of their own accord. When a guest arrives, they simply nod their heads and let him depart.
I show you, my junior Dharma-brother Fazhao:
this small hermitage cannot accommodate your stay. As we part by the lakeside, there is much lingering sentiment.
If you wish for your body and mind to attain long-lasting stability, remember the time you ate vegetables within the double enclosures.
Fayì said: "I once recalled the time when the city was falling and the barbarians were in pursuit;

looking back at Pingjiang as it was transformed into a field of rubble—this very moment was precisely where the mind comes to rest. The Master said: "How could it be merely a matter of resting the mind?"
Do not forget these three points; they are the true medicine. It is no hindrance to keep neither needles nor thread.
Only when you have thoroughly exhausted yourself like a chicken being scalded will it be time to begin Zen practice as a place of rest.
Hearing that Pingjiang is ablaze—A-he-he!
A-he-he! The entire settlement is like an anthill. A single flare of fire consumes it, leaving no trace;
how many people here have awakened to the dream of Nanke?
Yanqiang requests a verse:
"An old monk’s stay in this world shall not be long. You, my son, are in the prime of your years; you must straighten your spine like tempered steel.
Do not linger with bitter attachment to your native village."

To show how the Master’s diligent pursuit of renunciation reached its ultimate end: he transcended the dust of sensory emotions and conquered the enemy, the Mara of death. Do not seek only warmth and satiety within the monastic groves;
a hundred years of worldly life pass away in mere idleness.

To demonstrate the practice of a junior monk’s pilgrimage: the predecessors of old packed their bundles with the intent of minimizing external conditions; there was nothing superfluous or trivial, and no objects of luxury or play.
This is exemplified by Deshan, who traveled to Dayu with only a double-layered cloth bag. As for the way people pack their bundles today—
It is not like that at all. The alms bowl is placed in a bag made of plum-blossom-patterned cotton cloth;
the *cibu* (monastic robe) is kept in a pouch of ancient Shu brocade; the water flask is paired with a cushion, all of which must be bright and fresh.

The staff and the ritual knife must be elegant and well-crafted. On the top of the rain hat, decorative inscriptions and characters must weigh several catties; inside the lining, the socks are stitched with thread.
Such a needle case. To look at it as a whole load, one seeks only for others to say it is good, forgetting one's own diligent toil.
A truly liberated monk would certainly not act like this. In a casual manner, he carries his bundle;
with steadfast resolve, he acts as a man of the Way, just like a wild crane or a solitary cloud. One must take care not to—
To be without ropes yet bound by them—listen further to this verse from an ancient:
"The ancients kept but two needles; for summer they used hemp, for winter fur, seeking them as needed. You all are in the prime of life with sturdy feet;
you should carry a double-needle case and traverse the monasteries."
A Verse for Training Novice Monks at Zifu:
The mundane world is in turmoil, with no end in sight; To enter the Gate of Emptiness is the true advantage. One must strive with constant diligence day and night;
Do not merely pass the time in weary toil.

The mind-monkey is easily let loose—how can one restrain it? The horse of the will is difficult to tame—it must also be disciplined. Until old age, the dust of worldly passions cannot be swept away entirely;
I fear that as a renunciant, I shall find it hard to sustain the four requisites of life.

Burn incense and prostrate with no haste; let your eyes behold and your mind dwell upon the sacred countenance. Repent of the defilements and sins accumulated over many lifetimes, and pray that you may receive the Dharma-water to cleanse your heart and mind.
The conduct of one who has left the household life must accord with its precepts; remain ever vigilant, as if treading upon thin ice.
Although you have not yet removed your beard and hair, you must ensure that your every movement and demeanor are those of a monk.
One must also study calligraphy and recite the sutras. The mind-ground of one who has left the household life must be clear and distinct.
In years to come, on the day you don the shaven head and the square-cut robe, every matter will be spontaneously perfected as it arises.
If one who has left the household life does not cease from consuming pungent foods and alcohol, they are merely occupying the grounds of a monastery in vain.
If the field of the mind remains unpurified until old age, even the seeds of Bodhi will find it difficult to sprout.
Do not speak of the faults or virtues of others; speaking and speaking will bring calamity upon yourself.
If you can keep your mouth shut and deeply conceal your tongue, this is the foremost method for cultivating the self.

Not even a hair’s breadth of the eternally abiding [nature] may be stolen; though one might generate ten thousandfold daily, it would be difficult to repay. The heads of pigs and the feet of donkeys are clearly seen;
the ground of Buddhahood has not yet been swept clean in this life.
Do not emulate the foolish who speak empty falsehoods; such deceptive talk will eventually reach its end. Do not say in secret that no one sees you;
I fear it will be difficult to deceive Minister Ma.
First, one should leave the household life to become a disciple. Serve the teacher as if serving one's own parents in the hall. Be diligent and careful in adding incense and changing the water;
the various devas will surely witness and observe you.

Apply yourself with diligence in the Fragrant Accumulation Kitchen; the dragons and elephants of the Five Lakes dwell within the groves. Though it may be arduous to gaze upon the stars and the moon, you must believe that when the cause is profound, the fruit is likewise profound.
When the twice-daily communal labor is called, one should arrive early; with many hands, tasks can be accomplished without error.
One should recite a single scroll of the Tathāgata’s sutras, rather than filling one's mouth with idle chatter.

Encountering a monk in the corridor, inquire after him with deep respect; meeting a guest at the gate, call out to him with courtesy. One who has left the household life should maintain an attitude of humility and deference;
do not be like a fool who lacks proper etiquette.
Whether household items be fine or coarse, one should cherish them. When using them, regard them as if they were one's own eyes. Do not cast them about recklessly at will;
those who use things must know how difficult it is for them to be formed.
In providing for the various quarters, one must be diligent; in sweeping the floors and preparing incense, do not grow weary of the frequency.
If one can always be earnest and careful in serving the community, only then is one a true renunciant in body and mind.
One's robes, shoes, and socks must be kept neat and orderly; one must never be without a hanging cloth or bedding. One should always maintain the four dignified postures of the body;
do not follow the foolish by becoming coarse and negligent.
One must not engage in hand-to-hand combat; such coarse and boisterous behavior is not that of a renunciant. When spat upon by others, one must wipe it away;
ultimately, to yield to others is no sign of folly.
When entering the hall for the three-fold bathing drum, one must distinguish between the upper and lower robes regarding contact and purity. Speaking or laughing loudly is strictly forbidden;
do not let coarse conduct destroy your dignified demeanor.

Sometimes, following the trail to the street, one must tend the water-buffalo of Mount Mushi. Constantly tending it where the grass grows deep outside the gate, if it is lost for a moment, it is difficult to recover.
Your physical body is healthy; do not be greedy for sleep. Labor with diligence and press forward. Have you not seen the practitioner Lu of the mill?
It was he who transmitted the robe and bowl to the Patriarch’s Hall.
When meeting with Prime Minister Cai at Bianxi, he saw directly beneath him.
A single inch of clear blue eyes is like a flash of lightning; if one stirs even a moment of thought, it is more than a thousand mountains distant.
What need is there for a wall to face? The meditation seat is now turned around. I laugh instead at the dull Hu monk who cannot even take another breath.
This matter is inherently so: the spring scenery fills the imperial capital; as the dawn breaks upon the wine tower, the Great Vairocana is fully manifest.
Everywhere there are skillful means; how many can realize this principle? Failing to recognize Xuefeng’s ball, you mistakenly identify Salt Official’s fan.
Grand Master Sun, having sought a verse on governance, already rivals Minister Pei; in discussing Chan, he must surely laugh at the old Vimalakīrti. Since the Way exists, cease lamenting your return.
Late in the evening: A single word that strikes the vital point is already too much.
Residing again at Hui-lin, I rhyme with High Official He upon my return:
I sleep soundly and am too lazy to discuss the Truth; Let the Chan followers do as they please, whether they rejoice or grow angry. This has made Master Yutang laugh until his face is split.
[The Master] said: "A solitary cloud comes and goes according to the person. He replied:
"To have stayed overnight with you, Director Ge, on Mount Dongting—this karmic connection is no ordinary matter. One should well remember this one phrase before the lamp."
Child, do not let it wander and fall into the human world;
throughout the day, Perfect Enlightenment is never lost. Why labor in this life of toil, forcefully creating right and wrong?
Once the drifting clouds and every speck of dust are swept away, the moon within this heart will shine of its own accord.
Inscribed for Deputy Magistrate Sun’s Zhenqing Pavilion:
Yellow scrolls unfurled, one shares the Buddha’s words; Green mountains face us ever, accompanying the monk’s dhyāna.
As the incense in the single burner fades and the six periods pass, Who in this floating world possesses such karmic affinity?
The Academician Zhang took refuge at Maogong Mountain, where he styled himself the Layman Yinqian. He subsequently made an appointment to partake in the "Lushan Meal" (a vegetarian feast).
Carrying a staff and bearing a verse, he came to attend the Lushan Meal.
Seeing with joy that the Master’s garden contained vegetables, he mused: "How could the old man Longmian not have resided here?"
The Scholar. Danqing has again painted the "Hidden Spring" (Yinqian) scroll.
In mourning for Inspector Wang:
Last year you arrived at Baoshan Temple; we met beneath the trees and laughed without ceasing. Today I have come, but you are already gone.
Depart! The stone sheep and stone tigers cause people anxiety.
But at the moment of death, having once obtained the words of an old monk, one sweeps away the myriad affairs within the breast. Turning back on worldly glory, it all becomes like a dream;
thus one is able to speak with laughter even before the gates of death.

I thank Wáng Qī, the Palace Attendant, for bestowing upon me his own hand-copied copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as well as various scriptures from the Great Canon, including the image of Amitābha and the scroll of the *Mahāsāhasrapramardana Sūtra*.

The characters emerge like fine hairs from the tip of a brush; forged with iron yet possessing the elegance of silver hooks, every single stroke is pure and clear. Furthermore, one must realize this very point at the head of the matter.
A single dot emits radiance atop the heap of the six sense-objects;
the Great Dharma circulates through fifteen hundred springs. Even now, the Western Mountains have not yet recognized the golden script;
the jade-bound volumes and precious scrolls illuminate the crags and valleys, making one imagine that even the dragons and spirits rejoice.
Every day I behold the Buddha’s sublime form, just as when I saw you on the streambank. His majestic appearance is beyond both the mundane and the sacred;
it requires only that one does not lose one's way upon the path.
I have tied a thatched hut to enclose the mountain;

having grown old, I entrust myself to the retired life of Xu Yanfu, the District Magistrate. My provisions are exhausted, yet I have borrowed money to purchase Mount Dongting. Who among the court officials sends me three measures of rice?
Amidst wind and rain, I preserve my single thatched cottage. With a clear whistle, clouds part over the moonlit peaks; with a high sleep, no guests come to disturb me.

The gate of firewood is closed. Let me try to explain this state of mind to those who understand: it must be like being separated by the cold waters of the Canglang River, causing one’s countenance to break into a somber smile.

Having met with my elder brother in the secular world, our deep fraternal affection has long had its origins. On the divergent paths of life and death, each must cultivate his own way. If you wish to know what lies within the pit of the five desires—
Perilous! A single-leafed boat upon ten thousand acres of wind and waves.
Vice-Minister Yin, having completed the casting of the bell for Mount Bao, requested a verse.
At Mount Bao, once the bell was cast in a single firing, all things at the tips of the hundred grasses were entirely sound. This awakens the weary life and opens the sleep.
The Eye. At once, one attains clarity within this.
Official Li requested a verse:

"At the tip of the staff and beneath the brush, one must be precise; in striking the lock and knocking the shackle, apply your mind well. To become a Buddha or a Patriarch is nothing other than this."
This is it. I urge you not to seek elsewhere. Sun Baoyi, seek a verse to examine conditions and find contentment;
there is constant peace and joy therein. Excessive expenditure and much seeking damage the spirit of the Way. The Patriarch is at the gate of the bustling marketplace.
My mind is set; let me release it so that the ground of the heart becomes vast and level.
Layman Wu Baoyi requested a verse:
"Meeting you the other day, I was delighted by our cordial conversation; seeing the vast and level expanse within your breast, I realize the Patriarch has a way of entry."
Verse: If you simply keep all matters light during your time, Venerable Wang, I seek this verse to urge you:
do not pursue greed extensively. Satisfy your household needs as they arise, and then rest. How much of the light of a hundred-year life can there truly be?
A Day. It is better to turn back early when you find the place to turn back.
The new livelihood of Old Man Jin Da:
seeking verses, prostrating, and burning incense. The old family custom of his house: rowing a boat and planting tangerines. If you wish to know your own Amitābha—
The Buddha is none other than Old Man Geumdae of Hangsan. He granted his good friend a request for a verse and twenty mu of land to provide for the seasonal sacrifices.
Having neither wife nor concubine, he is a man of freedom; when he looks back upon his ten-thousand-mu fields of fertile soil, they appear as nothing more than a vast expanse.
This person is one who has many worldly affairs among men.

A good friend of his recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and sought to master it through recitation for forty years. As he grew old, his mind became increasingly focused and dedicated; I have encouraged him not to worry about life.
Death. This very practice is Zen; it is Zen. There is no need for investigation. A single phrase encompasses five hundred volumes.
Without self, without person, without a life-principle—dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, one laughs at Gautama.
While reading the Lotus Sūtra, upon reaching the Parable of the Burning House, I could not help but laugh. Thereupon, I wrote this verse to show my grandson, the District Magistrate:
"In my dreams, the calamity of fire was vividly clear; Upon waking, the mind-ground is fundamentally cool and refreshing. The three chariots were likewise intended for the children."
[The Master] said: "Suppose one were to imagine that there was another method for seeing Gautama.
A man of high attainment once said: 'Master Hui-lin’s informal discourse (xiaocan) says that this human body is a provisional combination, like a broken sand pot;
do not let it slip from your hands and shatter it, and you will immediately see the thousandfold rest and ten-thousandfold rest. The Master asked:"
“You sand bucket! How many years have you been used? Gao replied, “Sixty-three years.
The Master laughed and said, “Take care, take care!
This human body is just like a broken sand bucket; bound by three strips of bamboo, it is entirely temporary. As summer passes and winter comes, you should cherish it.”
"Alas! Do not let there be more mud upon the earth.
Gao heard this and tears fell from his eyes. The Master said, "There is something indestructible; do you recognize it?
Gao said, "I beg the Master for instruction."
The sand basin is shattered and turns to dust; only then is one truly a person who supports the heavens and upholds the earth.
The whole world speaks only of the body as an illusion, yet they do not know that it is someone within the illusion who speaks.
"Friends of the Way, because of your attachment to the Dharma, you constantly come to Mount Bao.
I have used verses to turn you away, for I, an old monk, am beset by many ailments and weary of receiving guests. For now, I shall go into seclusion on Western Mountain under an assumed name.
If you are a true friend of the Way from my own house, we shall meet most clearly across the lake."
When the patron of Shinshū has finished requesting this verse:
"Karmic obstacles are originally empty; the mind is like a swarm of ants, the intellect is like the wind. If you have not yet realized this, you must repay your past debts;
once the roof is torn away, it is covered again with thatch grass. The lanterns and the pillar laugh heartily—how wonderful is the mouth of Jiao!"
More: "I report that the waters at the head of the Yangtze River—do not stir up waves for no reason. (This person died within a few months due to official business.)
Zifú was renamed Shēnxiāo. His fellow practitioners tried to detain him, but the Master departed. He left behind this verse to bid them farewell:
The coming together and parting of people is fundamentally impermanent; Do not burden your mind and belly with idle sorrows.
In thirty years we shall meet again, Clapping our hands and laughing heartily.
The Supplementary Record of Master Cishou Shen,
Volume II:
Supplemental Verses Modeled after Hanshan (Twenty Poems in Total)
I love the man from Cold Mountain; though his body is poor, his mind is as it should be. He composes poems without regard for meter or rhyme; he has plenty of time left over from tending the fire.
His tattered, soiled clothes he is too weary to wash; his unkempt hair he is too lazy to comb. When we meet, he simply lets out a long whoop—how could those with fleshly eyes ever know him?

Shide’s poetry is pure and austere; the Way of *feng* and *sao* naturally endures within it. He gazes at clouds while singing by bamboo and stone; he walks under the moon as he emerges from the pine gate.
Recognize the seal within your heart; do not polish away the traces upon the mirror. At every moment there is much leakage; in this dusty world, few recognize gratitude.
Human life is like a floating plant upon the water; it flows and turns, becoming a river of craving. Stirred by the winds of ignorance, one enters and exits the waves of birth and death.

If, for even a single thought-moment, you know how to bring it to rest, all conditions will cease and demons vanish. You must urgently ascend to the shore of enlightenment; I urge you, my son, not to let this time slip away.

In human life, craving and attachment are heavy; what one desires is never fully satisfied. A single meal may suffice for fullness, yet with ten thousand measures of grain, the mind still finds no rest.
When will this dark karma ever end? Even the crimson skirt brings shame; the hair upon the head is already overtaken by snow, yet one still drifts through the days in idle leisure.
When has anyone ever eaten ten thousand coins? Yanzi drank from but a single ladle. The wise man’s mind dwells on the Way; the fool’s ambition lies in the kitchen.

The inclinations of the wise and the foolish differ so greatly—how much more so than the distance between clouds and mud! To be pampered and fed may not be a blessing; this truth is as clear as the light of day.

In human life, it is precious to be without worldly occupation; it is not precious to possess many skills and talents. While people may look upon such skills with favor, an occupation can bring calamity to one’s very form.
Though your literary works may be exquisite beneath heaven and your spirit may swallow the vast ocean, if this body is once lost, you shall drift aimlessly through the six realms of existence.
The clever people of this world surely desire to hear of my faults; how could they know that it is driven by karma? For the most part, greed brings about calamity.

Cause and effect are like reflections in a mirror; since the reflection is none other than myself, the retribution of the hidden realm is most distinct. How can one discuss the greatness of official rank?
Human life is like spring blossoms; for how long can it remain beautiful? Blown by the morning wind and washed by the evening rain, the rosy countenance turns withered and parched.
While fallen flowers may give rise to new growth, once a person has grown old, they never return to youth. Let all affairs rest for now; do not further invite affliction.
The people of the world fear speaking of death; as soon as they mention it, they avoid the subject. Yet when the time of death arrives, their aged eyes first fall with tears.
They cling to their wives and dote on their concubines, seeing gods and spirits alike. Failing to enter the Gate of the Patriarchs, they remain deluded and confused until the very end.
At sixty, cease building houses; at seventy, do not acquire clothing. Even if you were to enjoy these things, for how much longer could you do so?
You must bring rest to body and mind early, preparing yourself for the time of death. It is just as when a person travels far away: it is more convenient to prepare in advance.

The power of the Way and the power of merit appear similar in ordinary times, yet they seem to be confused. The power of merit has its ebbs and flows; the power of the Way knows neither wealth nor poverty.
If one does not study the Way during their human life, one merely plants the causes for saṃsāra. Behold those whose heavenly merit is exhausted: dust and grime fill their eyes.
I estimated for myself that I would reach seventy; how could I have expected such haste? Now, at fifty or sixty, my physical form feels gradually declining.
It is just like the end of spring, when the green is abundant but the red is scarce. Departure and staying are but a breath away—these words are truly not deceptive.
It is like facing a bright mirror, where face and features confront one another: the beautiful person rejoices silently within, while the ugly person likewise feels shame.
Yet the mirror remains indifferent to both, its luminous clarity ever of one essence. If the human mind were like this mirror, Buddhahood would be attained in the snap of a finger.
Elaborate funerals are not filial piety; the deceased will surely suffer dishonor. Behold these times of chaos and strife—what tomb has not been plundered?
The gold is divided among the many bandits, while the solitary soul cries out in the daylight. I most admire the elder Zhuang Zhou, for whom heaven and earth serve as a coffin.
One who has left the household life must reduce attachments; by reducing attachments, it is easy to enter the Way. How can those who claim to have no concerns repeatedly grasp at idle afflictions?
Rushing to the gates of wealth and honor, they adorn their dwellings with fine things, unaware that they are being driven by external objects. Thus they toil in vain until old age.
If one seeks to stop contention through contention, that strife will only increase and never cease. Only patience can bring contention to rest; this is the most noble quality within the Dharma.
When the ancient Gautama beheld the demonic armies approaching with swords and spears, he met them with nothing but a mind free of attachment.
If this human body were devoid of karma, what doubt would there be regarding birth and death? One need not cling to life, nor should one grieve for death.
This single body is but a true inn; all myriad affairs are but children’s play. Please come to the side of Green Rock, and let us sing together of the purple mushrooms.
I watch quietly as the swallows build their nests; with mud in their beaks, they turn a thousand times. One drop falls upon the beam of a poor man’s house; one settles for a night in a royal palace.

Their lodging is but for a brief moment—how could there be leisure to distinguish between noble and base? If people in life understand this principle, they will remain free of joy or resentment until the end of their days.

The poor find it difficult to cultivate merit; the wealthy easily commit transgressions. Those with power often lack the mind of the Way; those with the aspiration for the Way lack the necessary means.

Among those who possess both merit and the mind of the Way, there is not even one or two in a hundred. Had I not seen the Elder Gautama, whose merit and wisdom were both perfectly adorned and beautiful.

The Buddha is the Great King of Physicians; he has left behind the sutras to treat the myriad ailments of sentient beings. Although sentient beings read these sutras, they fail to apply them in practice one after another.
Illness consists of greed, hatred, and delusion; these must be swept away until they are utterly purified. If greed, hatred, and delusion are not eliminated, there is no way to realize true nature.
Preface to the Third Volume of the Extensive Record of Chan Master Cishou of Huilin Temple in Dongjing:

When Chan Master Cishou preached the Dharma and composed verses and hymns, he was like a great king of physicians who administers medicine according to the specific ailment; there was nothing in him that was perfunctory or superficial.

The world alike rejoiced to hear [his teachings] and delighted in propagating them. During the Master’s lifetime, when the assembly wished to carve his words into printing blocks, the Master personally forbade it.
He consequently commanded his attendant to collect all his private notes and burn them; thus, throughout the Master’s life, his recorded sayings (*yulu*) were never heard to have been published.
After the Master passed away, a Dharma-heir monk gathered the Master’s words from six different monasteries where he had served as abbot and compiled them.
I have compiled these into an upper and lower record, all consisting of dialogues held with monastics beneath the forest trees.

As for those instances where he played freely in the marketplace, speaking with unrestrained license so that sentient beings might attain understanding according to their kind—these are mostly not recorded here.

One day, while I was paying my respects at the teacher’s stupa, his disciples informed me: "The world universally acknowledges the virtue and character of our Master; there is no one who does not know of it."
It awaits future generations to bring it forth. Yet, as for the unfolding of his eloquence, it was like the thunder of spring resounding and the Milky Way pouring down in autumn.

What is transmitted today is thus concise; were it to be lost within a hundred years through private records, how could scholars who hear of its spirit find joy in it, and by what means would they verify it?
Now, wishing to collect the notes of my disciples and record them extensively, I have commissioned artisans.
He brandished his axe to instruct future students. I said: "What has been circulated previously already contravened the late teacher’s intent;
now that I have further collated it, the errors have become even more pronounced. His disciples said: "Not so. Master Yunmen..."
He preached the Dharma like clouds, yet he never permitted anyone to record his words; upon seeing such attempts, he would invariably scold and revile them.

At that time, Mingjiao used paper as clothing, and whatever he heard, he immediately recorded in writing. What is transcribed here within this "Room for Responding to Capacities" (Duījīshì) is all that has been passed down from him.
Had Mingjiao followed the words of Yunmen, the Ancient Tower Master (Gūtǎzhǔ) would have had no cause for awakening, and today—
In the monastic communities (seng-lin), one no longer hears what was spoken at that time.

We would rather disobey the admonitions of our late teacher than fail to ensure that future generations may hear them together. I said: "To reject the former and adopt the latter, I do not presume to know.
However, by citing the example of Mingjiao to circulate the words and phrases of our late teacher, fellow practitioners may perhaps find something of value herein. Thus it came about.

[He] spoke these words and [inscribed them]. On the day of the Lantern Festival in the year of Yimao (1135) of the Xiangshu era, at Huilin Chan Monastery in Dongjing, the Venerable Cishou Shen ascended the hall to deliver a verse on an ancient precedent.
Compiled by Attendant Pushao.

At the offering for the Sixth Patriarch, he ascended the hall and said: "Last night someone came to report that the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, the Second Patriarch Master Ke, the Third Patriarch Master Can, the Fourth Patriarch Master Xin, the Fifth Patriarch Master Ren, and the Sixth Patriarch Master Neng have come to visit the Chan Master.
The mountain monk then instructed them to be invited. Bodhidharma stepped forward, spread his sitting cloth, and said: 'For a long time...'"
I look up to the wind of the Way, yet have no means to pay my respects in person. The mountain monk grasps his sitting mat and says, "We are both old men; there is no need for such formality.
Bodhidharma gazes directly at the mountain monk and says, "Nine years of cold sitting atop Bear Peak; the five-petaled flower blooms as spring spreads across the great earth.
The mountain monk says, "Do not show off so much. The Second Patriarch says, "Behold the three feet of snow in the courtyard. He specifically—
The ground caused both of the man’s arms to grow cold. The mountain monk said, "Dull-witted teacher.

The Third Patriarch said, "Since you know that the nature of sin is fundamentally undefiled, with one punch you can topple Mount Wangong. The mountain monk said, "Save your eyebrows. The Fourth Patriarch said:

"Awakening brings liberation; there are no ropes or bonds. One fist overturned against the void attains freedom. The mountain monk said, "This is not yet the work of a master hand. The Fifth Patriarch said, "When returning as a youth to the place where the robe was transmitted, I recall once again the time I planted trees in a former life. The mountain monk said, "My poor brother thinks of old debts. The Sixth Patriarch said, "Do not follow the husks of threshed grain; you have no skill. It is within the mortar that the rice is pounded out. The mountain monk said, "A poor elder brooding over past obligations.
