"Old rhombus-flower. The mountain monk said, "It is better to be heavy than to be light. Bodhidharma said, "I, this old monk, traveled far across the whale-waves to reach this land.
Twice I was poisoned; I have experienced every kind of peril, hardship, and difficulty. As for those who come after me..."

Standing in the snow to sever one’s arm, planting trees and husking grain—these were done solely for this very matter. Yet nowadays, my brothers and fellow practitioners eat their fill and sleep soundly, refusing to study the Way.
It can be said that the true eye has recently been swept away like dust; it is difficult to find worthy descendants in the Chan gate.
The mountain monk let out a thunderous shout and said, "Dare you still dare to pant for breath? We people of this region are fundamentally without affairs.
Yet you have come here to speak nonsense and corrupt the sons and daughters of others' families. If you continue to chatter on like this, I shall drive you back over the Pamir Mountains;
do not say I did not warn you. Bodhidharma said, "The time since the Sage has grown distant, yet there are still elders such as this."
The mountain monk said, "What is there to say? There is. He then drove them all out of the abbot's quarters with his staff at once.
He called out again, "O sons of Chan! You six old fellows have been brought to your senses by me. Now you have no more business in your minds;
each of you, please return to the hall."
Ascending the hall to offer a vegetarian feast for his mother: Time flows swiftly, as rapid as a rushing stream. Since parting from your compassionate countenance, how many autumns have passed?
The graves and the homelands lie empty and distant; The diverging paths of life and death stretch long and wide. The kindness of nursing us to fill our hunger is hard to repay;
The strength required to carry this physical frame is beyond recompense. I imagine your voice and features, yet find no place to seek them; The spring breeze, by chance, brings this moment.
People are distressed. To speak in such a manner is very much like having not yet eliminated worldly vulgarity; it shows that the bonds of affection have not been severed.

But tell me, how will a monk repay this debt of gratitude? He then struck the ground once with his staff and said: "To offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the mother's kindness."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Nirvana and birth-and-death are two names; viewed through the true eye, they are but one enlightened nature.

When the clouds disperse atop the mountain of the five aggregates, the moon shines forever bright throughout the great chiliocosm. This segment of radiance illuminates heaven and mirrors earth, shining through antiquity and soaring into the present;
it has never lacked anything. Within this light, there is no birth or death, no coming or going, and no longevity or premature end."

There is no limit to success or failure. To see there is birth and death, to see there is coming and going, to see there is success or failure, or to see there is premature death or longevity—all these are seeing that the dark clouds have not yet dispersed atop the mountain of the five aggregates. Therefore it is said: "Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.
When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-faculties are removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfectly pure. Even if you reach this state, [it is still not enough].
Furthermore, you must know that there is the monk’s staff before you can succeed. Now tell me: what is the monk’s staff?
After a long silence, he said: "The edict that is not transgressed."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddhas did not appear in the world, nor did they turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma three times.
The Patriarchs did not come from the West. A single phrase pervades the entire world. This one phrase is the sturdy boat for crossing the sea of birth and death.
This one phrase is the great bright lamp that shatters the darkness. This one phrase is the excellent medicine that cures all ailments."
A single phrase is the sharp axe for felling the tree of afflictions. The Buddhas of the three periods of time have transmitted this single phrase;
the patriarchs of the six generations have transmitted this single phrase. The entire Great Canon of teachings, consisting of five thousand and forty-eight fascicles, [is nothing other than this].
All of these flow forth from this single phrase. But tell me: from what place does this one phrase flow?
After a long silence, he said: "If you attempt to calculate it with the faculty of thought, you will never reach its end."
Ascending the hall, incense was burned and the drum struck; questions and challenges were exchanged with unrestrained vigor. The Great Gate of Giving is open, and truth is revealed at every turn.
Even moths, insects, and ants all expound upon suffering and emptiness; the pillar and the lantern both discourse on Prajñā.

Such direct pointing is intended specifically for the present age, yet to observe from a side-eye perspective is not yet stable or correct. When a monk reaches this point, he must know that there are three things.
This is a place where the physical forms of all the Buddhas of the world cannot reach; a place where the six generations of Patriarchs could not transmit or receive [the Dharma];
a place where the old monks of the world cannot grasp. If you can penetrate this point, you will attain great mastery within the realm of birth and death.
If you cannot penetrate it, speaking of food will never satisfy your hunger.

Ascending the hall for the commencement of the summer retreat: The three-month *an-guo* (summer retreat) is essential for protecting life; Silkworm moths, crickets, ants, and insects swarm about in confusion.
But the patch-robed monk has his own path for turning around; He does not walk where worldly people walk. After a long silence, he said:
"Under the three rafters, the pure breeze is far-reaching; Before the six-foot mat, the bright day is long."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The plantain tree opens upon hearing thunder—does it have ears? The sunflower turns toward the sun—does it have eyes?
The mulberry tree of the village-spirit knows the wind from heaven—does it have a mind? The ocean water knows the cold of heaven—does it have intention?
Even insentient things still know the seasons for themselves; yet how many monks are there who remain perpetually in a state of drowsy stupor?"
Ascending the hall for the communal labor of hauling earth. At Zifu, the way of teaching others has never had an alternative path.
When one’s meal is finished, it is as if one is at leisure; together we haul several loads of earth. You walk, and I also walk; you stop, and I also stop.
If you understand this, how extraordinary! Even if you do not understand, I grant you my approval. Since you do not understand, why do I grant you my approval? Although so, you have not attained it.
The strength [of this] still surpasses other labors of mind.
As the ox ascends the dais, one cries out: "Alas! This body of a different species revolves without rest; bearing horns and covered in hair, it suffers in its distress to repay human labor.
I observe that the Buddha and the ox are, by their very nature, originally one. It is truly because of being deluded regarding this mind that..."

Because your physical form has changed so drastically, when you were a human being, how could you have imagined this day? You embezzled funds belonging to the Sangha and misappropriated the property of the universal community.
You spoke of right and wrong with reckless abandon and indulged in wine and meat at will. Since you did not observe the five precepts, how could you have attained a human body?
Today, having fallen into the body of an ox, you finally realize that [your past actions] brought no benefit.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In the school of the Patriarchs, the root source is directly pointed out; it speaks only of seeing one's nature to become a Buddha.
Beyond this, there are various divergent doctrines. As for the principle of seeing one's nature to become a Buddha, each resides within the individual's own sphere—vivid, solitary, and luminous."
It is like the sun illuminating the day, like the moon illuminating the night; fundamentally, it is never obscured. Therefore it is said: "All sounds are the Buddha’s voice;
there is no other sound. All forms are the Buddha’s form; there is no other form. Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he asked, "Do you hear?
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara is turning the Great Dharma Wheel right inside your ears. He then raised [the whisk] again.
Raising his whisk, he said: "Do you see? Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is upon your eyebrows, emitting light and shaking the earth.
Nevertheless, even though this is so, you must further realize that there is a matter beyond seeing and hearing, transcending sound and form, before you can truly attain it."
Tell me this: what is this matter that transcends seeing and hearing, and cuts off sound and form? Do you understand?
Wait until empty space nods its head, and then I shall tell you.
Ascending the hall, he said: "It is just the beginning of midwinter, yet before we know it, the month is half gone. Time passes as swiftly as a shuttle; human affairs are as frantic as a drill.
White hairs increase upon the temples; ruddy cheeks are secretly exchanged for pallor. Fame and profit are vied for with headlong competition, yet no one observes the true matters.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, even if you were an iron man—why is it so? After a long silence, he said: [The Master remained silent.]
The seeds of the awakening flower exist, yet no one plants them; the fire of the mind is smokeless, burning day after day.
When Chan Master Yin accepted the invitation to Mount Jiangshan, he passed through Zifu Temple and ascended the hall for the discourse: "The Chan school is currently like drifting clouds;

from north of the Yangtze to south of it, they guard the vital passes. Do not blame the assembly for remaining idle and unprepared; we must sweep away the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to meet the needs of people."
"Great assembly, do you still see the new Abbot of Jiangshan? His mind-jewel is brilliant, his bearing is lofty and clear;

with a rhinoceros-horn crown and thick eyebrows, eyes like the Yellow River and a mouth like the sea, he brandishes his fly-whisk and looks down upon all quarters, [surveying] the six sites of enlightenment."

Even the thousand sages of the level shoulders [of Mount Tai] were surpassed; how much more so this magnificent site of Zhongshan, the upper reaches of Jiangnan. This is the field of awakening for Master Baogong and the meditation chamber of Prince Xu.
The Dharma seat has long been vacant, and today we rejoice that a worthy successor has been found. Disciples from across the four seas look toward this place with admiration and reverence.

Moreover, at this present time, when the patriarchal wind is failing and the teachings of the Buddha are on the verge of sinking, those who merely assume titles and occupy positions without merit seem...
Those who shake the collar and grasp the main thread are not one in ten thousand—among those as numerous as hemp seeds.

I further hope that you, Master Uncle Chan Master, will lower your demeanor and yield to human sentiment, thereby attracting those yet to come and circulating the True Eye. Who other than you could cause the Way of Perfect Illumination to shine resplendently throughout the world?
As for me, your junior nephew Zifu, my spiritual practice is unworthy and my character is clumsy and inept.
There are others who have recently inherited this tradition; for the most part, they possess nothing at all. All matters are desolate, and their meager conditions are truly lamentable.

It is a special honor that the Zen Master has graced us with his presence like a majestic elephant-king. Since the old shop is being opened by a mere child, why begrudge a performance upon this stage?

[The assembly] descends from their seats and entreats the Zen Master to briefly ascend this seat and let out a great thunderous roar, so that this entire assembly may hear what they have never heard before.
I have heard that such talk is still something known to everyone. But tell me, what about the principle that "six ears do not share a secret"?
Do you remember how one day Master Mihu led his assembly to visit Puzhi?
As soon as they met, Puzhi pulled his meditation seat around and sat down. Mihu stood behind him for a short while, and then returned to the guest quarters.
Ji said, "One must verify it before it is acceptable. He then had the attendant invite Mihu.
As soon as Mihu arrived, [Ji] pulled his meditation seat around and sat down. Ji walked once around the meditation seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Mihu led the assembly out. The Master said, "Observe how the ancients met one another; they never used worldly conventions to propagate the Dharma—not even a single needle or a single..."
Memorandum. To go from darkness and come into light is the spontaneous cultivation of the extraordinary. Although it is thus, one cannot avoid being short of a single move.
Among the assembly, some deliberate that when Pujie pulled over the meditation seat, he turned it into something superfluous.
Others say that because Mihuo stood behind Pujie, it resulted in a contrived fabrication. Still others say that as soon as he saw the meditation seat being pulled over, he immediately...
[He] overturned it. Furthermore, some say: "Just lift up the sitting mat and strike with the back of the arm. To handle the matter in such a manner is very much like a violent tiger;
on what basis? Such carelessness is extreme. If one were to examine this in its subtle, hidden depths, [the distance between them] would be vast indeed.
Since it is not so, tell me: how shall you deliberate upon this? If you all wish to see it clearly, you must have the Chan Master of New Jiangshan provide his critical judgment.
The bells chime as he ascends the hall. Wishing to forge the hundred-fold refined gold of the red furnace, he first requests that you all join together in a vast gathering of hearts.
For those who have long suffered upon the mountain of blades and the forest of swords, it would be well to produce wondrous sounds for the sake of weary beings.

"Great assembly," he said, after a long silence, "suppose there were a person here who was blind, deaf, and mute; how could one save them? After another long pause, he said: "The Buddha’s hand cannot block them; human hearts are naturally equal."
Xian. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the past, there were a thousand ways of speaking; today, upon examination, not a single one exists.
Only by casually turning over empty space can one finally attain lifelong enjoyment. As for this very empty space—how do you turn it over? It changes your eyes and pierces through them."
[The Master] ascended the hall and said, "Your nostrils! A former master once said: 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me.
Now, consider the lanterns, the pillars, the pure water jars, and the incense burners before us—these are all but objects. How can they become one body?"
"Go! Do you understand? Be careful not to add more mud to the ground. He ascended the hall.
"Maitreya, the true Maitreya, manifests a thousand billion emanations. The Master stepped down from the meditation seat, walked several paces, and then returned to his seat, saying:
"From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet people themselves fail to recognize him. If you can recognize him, Jiaoshan [is here] now."

The day was lost. The Master of Transformations was sent up to the hall. In the days of old at Jiaoshan, over a hundred people sat in the hall; winnowing baskets and wooden ladles were sufficient for their needs.
Today they are no longer enough to use. Great thanks to all you practitioners of Zen: each extend a hand, whether from the south, north, east, or west.
Facing south, one looks at the Northern Dipper; in the kitchen is a single cauldron. The porridge being cooked is not much, yet who could manage it were it not for Elder Xian?
Water Terrace meets with the street-wardens; six men serve as leaders. Simply observe the first and second months.
Night after night, incense and flowers are offered with a single-minded devotion. They strike the perimeter to plant vegetables;
their intent lies at the edge of the hoe. Both outcomes are equally successful. In the twelfth month, cold as ice, the assembly of monks still sleeps upon mats. The two men go out to beg for mats.
Gusu is not far away. The lacquer bucket must be broken. Deep Chan, however, requires radiance. Simply ensure there is no leakage;
even if you attain something, it does not matter. The radish from Zhenzhou is scarce everywhere this year. Master Qi goes to strike for money.
The kitchen steward laughed heartily. Little monk Fazhen, go find the cow of Mount Huai. You must hold the rope-head tight; you must firmly grasp the nostrils.

When the tracks are there, the cow is still there; with no-mind, it is ultimately easy to seek. If you wish to obtain it perfectly, [The cow] is right here. The tracks are there, and the cow is still there. If one is without mind, it is ultimately easy to seek. If you wish to attain it fully and well, [you must act thus].
Another story: there is another matter that is neither small nor large; it cannot be split apart, yet it can pass through even when one is barefoot.
It is ever present within daily activities, yet no one has been able to take it up and carry it. If you are willing to resolve your mind [to seek it], [then you may].
I shall explain it for you.
[The Master] ascends the hall. He cites a monk who asked Yunmen, “What is the One Song of Shaoyang? Yunmen said, “The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth lunar month.
The monk said, “If a student were to go forth in this very way, what then? Yunmen said, “For now, proceed slowly. The Master then—
He said: "O good people! Though those who sing [the song] are many, those who truly understand it are extremely few.
Often, you may grasp where this monk posed his question, yet you do not understand Yunmen’s response. Today, I, Jiaoshan, shall for your sake truly sing a single melody of Shaoyang."
The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month. Twenty-five staffs, twenty-five lanterns, twenty-five whisks.
For the general labor of planting vegetables, I ascend the hall. Jiaoshan has no special views of his own; he simply follows the ancients in planting vegetables.
Even if none of them take root, it is still a matter of merit for all of you. Without cause, you weary yourselves as dead Zen monks, merely wishing to stubbornly maintain [the tradition].
The boundaries: suddenly, when one encounters them head-on, one sees the "grass bandits" utterly defeated. Generally speaking, in practicing this matter, one must be free and at ease;
let the dust cover one’s face and the ashes smear one’s head, and fear neither wind nor sun. In old age, my intent lies in the hoe;
the family style naturally has the love of those who understand.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: At the end of summer, Dongshan addressed the assembly, saying, "All of you, at the beginning of autumn and the end of summer, you must go to a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass.

Later, a monk cited this to the Hermitage Master of Liuyang, who said, "Why did you not say, 'As soon as one steps out the door, it is grass'? The Master then said, "This fellow Dongshan has a mouth but no tongue-tip."
The words ceased. Master Xiaodao of Liusang said, "To stir up the turbid and raise the clear; I am particularly fond of the saying: 'Within a phrase, there is a phrase.
Master Cishou said, 'All of you, at the end of summer in early autumn, there are six paths. One path may be traversed; five paths may not be traversed.
First, do not press your eyes upon the ground of sacred subtlety so that flowers bloom before you.'"
Second, one must not recognize a servant as a lord upon level, ordinary ground. Third, one must not play with the remnants of rice and gruel at the gateway of luminous objects.
Fourth, one must not hide a blade and evade arrows within a chamber of non-action. Fifth.
One must not speak of yellow or red within the thicket of entanglements. Only upon the sixth path may all people proceed.
But tell me, how does one travel this path? Do you understand? Were it not for the straw sandals, who would realize the length of the road?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Do not say that being without mind is itself Chan. Within this, there is a path even more profound and mysterious.
Once the hitching post for the donkey has been overturned, striking the south sets the north in motion."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "All dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unceasing. If you can understand it in this way, the Buddhas are ever present before you.
You all should take the very mind that daily runs about in pursuit of things and investigate this matter. After a long time, it will naturally become clear.
If you do not do so, it is all nothing but a life lived in vain and a death met in delusion. Have you not seen the ancients?"
The Human Path: One must strive in this present life to bring it to completion; do not allow yourself to suffer the remaining calamities of future kalpas.
At the request of Marshal Liu, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Even where there is no elegance, there is elegance: a single horse chasing the wind across the four hundred prefectures."
The golden-tipped arrow leaves the bowstring after a hundred battles; the iron whip possesses great strength yet laments having no enemy.

O Great Assembly, this matter is like the principle of tightening one's defenses at the rear while seizing the banner before the army: in the mere interval of a deliberation, one has already missed the mark.
I, this mountain monk, have established a firm encampment at the heart of the Yangtze River, beneath Mount Haimen.
With Linji as my vanguard and Deshan as my rearguard, I don the armor of the Three Mysteries and array the banners of the Five Ranks.
I set up the bow of Shigong, wield the sword of Lingyun, beat the war drums of Heishan, and brandish the sturdy pitchfork of Bimozhi. At the crown of my head...

The True Eye illuminates heaven and earth; the golden mallet within the sleeve startles Buddhas and patriarchs. With the probing staff and the shadow-grass, one must strike the mark and act immediately.
Entering death and being born again—only then is this the skillful means of a true master.
Even so, tell me: who is it that does not move a blade of grass yet sits planning within the tent? After a long silence, he said: "When the arrow hits the red heart, people must not [doubt]."
Question: "The whole assembly is singing the Song of Great Peace.
Lay patrons, you have made offerings to the fifty-three spiritual friends of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; please ascend to the hall. Do you all see?"
Within the realm of Vairocana, True Suchness and conventional truth interpenetrate; within the Flower Treasury Ocean, all Buddhas and sentient beings are of one essence.
Throughout the three periods of past, present, and future, there is neither after nor before; the minds of ordinary beings and sages are one, without delusion and without awakening.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: "How marvelous! I now see that all sentient beings universally possess the Tathāgata."
The marks of wisdom and virtue are not realized solely because of deluded thoughts and attachments.

Thus, without departing from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he ascends to the Hall of Universal Radiance; and without leaving the Hall of Universal Radiance, he ascends throughout the heavens of Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, Tuṣita, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, proclaiming the nature of the Dharma-realm and preaching the Avataṃsaka Sūtra to cause all sentient beings [to attain realization].
Within one’s own body, one attains the vision of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtues, and marks.
For this reason, the youth Sudhana visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) without ever departing from his original resolve;

though he traversed over one hundred and ten great cities, he never once lifted a single step. If you wish to see the tenfold gates of the Dharma-realm and the tenfold Flower Treasury Oceans, [you must look within].
"The immeasurable becomes one; one is all, and all is one. He then picked up his whisk and said, "Realize it all at once right here!
Do you understand? At the peak of the Wondrous Mountain, quickly turn your head back; before the hall of the Ancient Buddha, fix your gaze. The Master spoke again:
"The Excellency has long dwelt within the nature-sea of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, throughout its seven locations and nine assemblies..."

Students, however, are often coarse-minded and mostly miss the mark right before their own eyes.
If you all can understand it here, King Xinguo did not leave his domain, yet he constantly saw Hui-lin; Hui-lin did not descend from his meditation seat, yet he was always with the King.
They meet face to face. Thus it is said: "Dīpaṃkara beckoned from afar at Golden Ground; the Wise One nodded silently at Jiangling.
Should this not yet be so, I, this clumsy mountain monk, offer a verse to celebrate the Great King’s longevity: "The spring colors within the cave are fine throughout the four seasons."

"Beyond the clouds, the peaks and ridges rise in a single expanse of height. May I pray for the life-span of the Worthy King, as long as that of the tortoise and the crane; year after year, let us gaze with clear eyes upon the peaches of immortality.
With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Closing the furnace, the Master ascends the seat and says: "Just as we have seen the opening of the furnace, now it is closed again. Cold comes and summer passes in but a moment.
The remaining snow before the courtyard has just melted away, yet the spring clouds upon the ridge have already unfurled.

Before our eyes, there is no dharma outside the mind; how many have ever awakened to the pearl within the topknot? The Patriarchs have never failed to offer these earnest instructions; it is simply that people of this age fail to see them."
This concerns the coarse level. The Way of the Patriarchs can only be known through direct realization; if one is not the right person, it will instead become mere frivolous discourse.
Therefore, the Buddha-dharma takes the mindless as its essence and the gateless as its gateway. As for this gateless gate, you must simply enter it.
The mind that is no-mind must culminate in wondrous awakening. Therefore, the red flowers and green willows are none other than the pure Dharmakāya;
the sounding of drums and the ringing of bells are entirely the mark of the broad and long tongue. Magnificent though this gateway is, those who advance through it are rare;
distinct though these sounds are, those who listen well are few. As the Patriarch said: "When responding to the ear, one is like a deep valley, [receiving] all sounds, great and small."
There is no insufficiency. Throughout the ten directions, bells and drums sound all at once; the numinous light vibrates in resonance, constantly continuing.
The Master strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and asks, "Do you hear it? Yuantong asked, "Greatly opening [the way], what matter separates clouds from mud?"
The donor requested the Master to ascend the seat. The Master said: "Standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high, one turns the wheel of birth and death beneath the heels;
cutting off all manifold differences, one presses out the Vajra-eye from the crown of the head—bright as the clear sun and swift as a hair-cutting blade.
Beyond seeing and beyond hearing, it is manifest and majestic in the presence of all. Yet, even though this is so, you must further know that there is the monk’s staff of killing and giving life."
Only then can you grasp the staff. What is this "monk’s staff of killing and giving life"?
In the sea of afflictions, use this staff as a boat and oar. On the perilous and evil paths, use this staff as a candle and a lamp.
If the Buddhas of the three periods had not possessed this staff, with what would they have saved sentient beings? As for the six generations of patriarchs...

If there were no such staff, with what would one transmit the Dharma? If the old monks throughout the land had no such staff, with what would they examine people? If you all had no such staff, with what would you come and go?
If the monastery itself had no such staff, with what would it serve its ruler and benefit the people, or carry out the practice of serving one's parents?
Xiao. Since each of you possesses this very staff, why is it that when questioned, you cannot bring it forth?
It is simply because you have been separated from it for too long and have let it lie buried for too much time; you are unwilling to accept its responsibility and you hide it from yourselves.
Have you not heard it said: "Picked up and put down without hindrance; struck once, and a thousand doors and ten thousand gates open?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "To return to the root and attain the essential meaning, seek the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses.

To follow after illumination and lose the source, look for your nostrils beneath the three rafter-poles. Long ago, a monk asked Zen Master Zhaozhou, 'The myriad dharmas all return to the One; where does the One return?
Zhaozhou replied, 'I was making a cotton shirt in Qingzhou that weighed seven catties. There are some who, upon hearing this..."
To raise the matter in such a way and then say, "Zhaozhou asked east and answered west; he did not abide in any fixed pattern," is already to fail the Master’s hand.
But tell me, where lies Zhaozhou’s essential intent? After a long silence, he said: "Water is known to be pure because of the moon;
the sky is seen to be high when there are no clouds."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Zen Master Hongjue, "Ultimately, how should one act as a member of the Sangha? Hongjue said, "It is good to dwell in the mountains.

The monk then prostrated. Hongjue asked, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "An ordained person remains as immovable as a mountain amidst the realms of good and evil, adversity and favor, and birth and death.
Hongjue then struck him, saying, "You have brought shame upon the ancient sages; you have lost me!"
Jue asked a monk standing nearby, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "The eyes do not see the colors black and yellow;
the ears do not hear the sounds of strings and flutes. Jue struck him again, saying, "You have brought shame upon the former sages and lost your own descendants.
The Master said, "Where a man of the Way proceeds, it is like fire melting ice. On the bird-path and the mysterious way, there is a path for turning back. This...
If a monk is a true man of the Way, as soon as he hears [the master] say, "How do you understand this? he should simply say:
"The Master plows with the sword; the student sows with fire. "The Master brews tea; the student sweeps the floor.

If one can deliver such a turning word, then even if Old Hongjue’s gate is as deep as the sea and his Way is as weighty as a mountain—his voice, countenance, and physical form being inviolable—it will be of no consequence.
One must also be taught until one’s entire face is covered in smiles.
He ascended the hall and, citing Muzhou’s instruction to the assembly, said: "If you have not yet attained a point of entry, you must attain a point of entry.
Once you have attained a point of entry, do not fail this old monk. A monk came forward, bowed, and said: "I, [the monk], shall ultimately..."
"I dare not fail the Master," [the monk] said. The State Governor (Zhaozhou) said, "You have already failed me.
The Master asked, "In what way did this monk fail? Another said, "This monk was not right to come out and prostrate; suppose he had not come out to prostrate."
Is it a failure? Or is it not a failure? Even if you do not step out [of this state], you still fail the ancients.
How can one avoid failing them? To reach this point, one must be a true person;
there is no way for those who merely speculate within the realm of conscious intellect or calculate over words and phrases to succeed. Do you know why Muzhou spoke thus?
This is already to have betrayed the multitude. Can you all discern this? An old woman, at the point of death, bids farewell three times;
lacking the "sinew" in her eyes, she has been poor for a lifetime.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example: A monk visited Zhaozhou, who happened to be sitting with his patched robe covering his head.
The monk then withdrew. Zhaozhou said, "Dharma brother, do not say that the old monk did not respond to you.

Another monk asked Fayan, "I beg the Master to extensively open up expedient means and provide an entrance for this student. Fayan then clapped his hands once. The Master said, "If you people want..."
Do you understand the intent of these two venerable masters? It is like sweeping and sprinkling a path clean to escort someone to their destination;
yet the person simply refuses to set foot upon it. When they suddenly do set foot there, what then? Compassionate Receptor (Cishou Sǒu) will carry your water jar and hold your alms bowl for you.

Wang Shu Gu shushen requested the Master to ascend the hall. Buddha to Buddha, hand is passed; this is the sole function. Patriarch to Patriarch, it is transmitted; one only clarifies this very thing.
If this is penetrated, the cycle of rebirth ceases; if this is not penetrated, it is the cause of birth and death.
Therefore it is said: "If you do not realize this meaning, your cultivation will be in vain and merely bitter toil.
If you were to look here, your thousand eyes would open at once, and you would perceive everything all at once. Walking is this very thing; sitting is this very thing.
Whether in anger or joy, in movement or stillness, in every action, nothing transcends this principle. It is like the yellow of gold or the azure of the blue sky—there is nothing else."
There is not even a hair’s breadth of difference between them. Nevertheless, although this is so, you must know that there is a path that goes beyond [this] before you can attain it.
What is this path that goes beyond? "A man of spirit naturally possesses the will to pierce the heavens; do not walk where the Tathāgata has walked. The Master spoke again:
"When Śāriputra entered the city, he encountered Candrottarā going out of the city. Śāriputra asked: 'Where are you going?'"

[Śāriputra] departs. The girl Candrottarā says, "If Śāriputra departs in such a manner," Śāriputra replies, "I have just entered the city, while you have already left it; how can you say that Śāriputra departs in such a manner?
The girl asks, "In what should a disciple of the Tathāgata abide? Śāriputra replies, "One should abide in accordance with *nirvāṇa*. The girl says, "A disciple of the Tathāgata..."
"Disciple, you should dwell in accordance with the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. I am just like Śāriputra; I have gone in this manner.
The Master said, "Although she is but a woman, she truly possesses the bearing of a man. Nevertheless, as it stands, neither of them yet possesses the nostrils of a patch-robed monk (*śramaṇera*).
I dare ask you all: where is it that they do not yet possess the nostrils of a patch-robed monk? Please inquire further."

When Chan Master Yuanwu was at Baogong’s pagoda, the pagoda manifested a sign. An official of the prefecture requested him to ascend the seat. The Master said: "The precious seal of Vairocana is fully manifest everywhere;
the adamantine eye is revealed at every turn. There is not a single person who does not possess it, nor is there a single dharma..."
Yet it is not something that can be fully accomplished through effort. Encompassing a hundred circuits and a thousand layers, it penetrates from the crown of the head to the very depths of the feet.
Therefore it is said: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing; yet by the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests within the world.
Sometimes it manifests as the body of a high official, sometimes as the body of a bhikṣu. From within a single eye, eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes flow forth; or from a single arm...
From within [the body], eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms are manifested; or, from a single face, twelve faces of supreme excellence are emanated.

He rescues suffering beings upon hearing their cries and gazes upon people with eyes of compassion. Like a valley responding to an echo, and like a mirror manifesting reflections, he unties the urgent distress of sentient beings hanging head-downward and supports the world against its perilous state, like a stack of eggs. At all times, he exhaustively fulfills the needs of the aged.
The compassionate heart. Everywhere one must clarify this one point. At this very moment, how do you express it in a single phrase?
"Atop the Peak of Solitary Dragon grows rootless grass; it scatters as spring throughout the great land of Jambudvīpa."

On the anniversary of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he ascended the hall and said: "The Great Awakened World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa two thousand years ago on the fifteenth day of the second month.
Today, his disciples, whenever they reach this time, give rise to feelings of sorrow and longing. I venture to ask you all:"
Now tell me: did he truly enter extinction, or did he not? Only if you can definitively determine this will you clarify the essential purport of the Buddha-dharma.
If you cannot definitively determine it, then even Pāpīyān would have to knit his brows in frustration. Recall how Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty asked Zen Master Rumang of the Western Capital:
"From what direction did the Buddha come? To what direction does he go when he passes away? Since you have already said...
[The Master asked: "The Buddha has long been in the world. Where is he now? Man said: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and returns to the unconditioned upon passing away.
The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it eternally abides in the place of no-mind. The Master said: "Excellent. Longya said:
"If you wish to attain Buddhahood easily, a mind free of thought (*amanasikāra*) is more than sufficient. Even so, for what reason [did the monk ask]?"
A monk asked Dongshan, “What is the Buddha? Dongshan said, “Three pounds of flax. A monk asked Shoushan, “What is the Buddha?

Shoushan said, “The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it. At this point, how shall we harmonize these? How shall we deliberate upon them? Listen to Jiangshan’s commentary:
“The most wondrous among the wondrous, the most profound among the profound; one must believe that within the alchemical flask there is another heaven.”
The iron tree blooms as the spring airs arrive early; at dawn, wind and rain fill the mountains and rivers.
Zen Master Zhiren, presiding over a water-land ceremony to dedicate merit for the late monk Xing of Jinshan, ascended the hall. He cited a verse by Master Linjiang, which says:
"In the second month of next year, the four elements will cast each other off; white bones shall scatter upon the Long River, sparing the donor from [the burden of]..."
On the day of his passing, he ascended the seat. A monk asked, "The clouds grieve and the mists darken; the great assembly cries out in lamentation.
We beg for a single word. Yang lowered one foot. The monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then the Dharma-mirror does not appear in this land?"
"Where else does the Jewel Moon shine? Yang replied, "It is not within your realm. The Master pressed him further: "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, yet it returns to the water;
the master departs and the master comes—this is simply the constant way. Yang shouted, "At the moment of departure, do not speak further!"
He withdrew his feet and immediately manifested a transformation. The Master said: "Tell me, what kind of principle did the ancients possess that they could come and go as they pleased?
If you say there was a principle, flowers will grow in your eyes; if you say there was no principle, flowers will grow in your eyes."
"Ultimately, what is it like? The Master struck his knee once and said: "To be poor at home is not yet poverty; to be poor on the road brings one to the brink of death.
Yesterday, when the bandits arrived at Mount Jinshan, the cruelty was such that it was truly unbearable to hear.

Master Xianzhong Min and the assembly of monks in the hall were all victims of their murderous hands; their livers and brains were smeared upon the ground, and blood filled the mountain. What kind of karmic conditions led to this?"
The karmic conditions converge here today. The Venerable Zhenren has specifically emptied his robes and bowl to prepare this vegetarian feast in commemoration.
I pray that all virtuous people may realize the fundamental emptiness of birth and death, and understand the equality between enemies and kin.

In the past, when Chan Master Shenguang went down the mountain to attend a feast, he encountered bandits on the road. As the bandits were about to strike him with their blades, Shenguang said, "I do not fear death."
"Yesterday, I suddenly accepted an invitation for a vegetarian feast from a lay devotee. Unable to fail my word, I allowed myself to be killed by you while I was away.
The bandit agreed. Once I had returned, I went to the bandit and let him kill me. When the bandit had departed, Guàn took the severed head and reattached it to the neck.
I have now slowly returned. He beat the drum and ascended the hall, saying: "Do all of you hear this headless [corpse]?"
Someone asked, "Does a person preach the Dharma? After a long silence, his head fell off. Only then did the assembly realize he had been killed by a thief.
The Master said, "Tell me, what samādhi was this? Now that he has been cut into two pieces by a single blow, who is it that picks up the head and places it upon the shoulders?
Who is it that preaches the Dharma? If you can understand this, only then will you know the destination of birth and death. No.
One knows for oneself the destination of one’s own birth and death; one also knows the destination of Chan Master Shen-guan.
Not only does one know the destination of Chan Master Shen-guan, but one also knows the destinations of all the brothers at Jinshan.
Now tell me: where do all these Chan practitioners go? Is it not like a boat traveling that depends on the steersman? Is it not so?
Is it like a mass of foam drifting with the wind? Or is it just like cutting through the spring breeze?
Neither of these is the principle. Old monk Cishou shall offer you a turning word: it is just like five hundred arhats crossing the sea, each displaying their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Those with great powers ride dragons and span phoenixes, moving with sovereign ease and leisure; those with lesser powers simply...
Thus, one should float the cup upon the sea to swiftly ascend to the other shore. Those without supernormal powers cannot avoid dragging through mud and water, resulting in a scene of total disorder.
I humbly entreat you to take care of yourself.

The Extensive Record of Master Cishou Shen, Volume Four;
Verses on Ancient Cases, Part Two.
Attendant Pushao recorded this case concerning Ānanda’s question to Kāśyapa:
"Aside from the golden robe transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda!
Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate."
Dhūta Kāśyapa and the learned Ānanda join their palms and raise their fists; brother and brother, difficult to match, suddenly encounter one another on a narrow path.
Their eyes bulge with rage as they find no place to hide; they topple the flagpole before the gate. A man of true character possesses the ambition to pierce the heavens.
Whenever Baizhang ascended the hall, there was always an old man who would follow the assembly to listen to the Dharma. One day, after the session had concluded, the old man did not leave.
Baizhang asked him, "Who is standing there? The old man replied, "I am no ordinary person.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in a past life, I once lived on this mountain. A monk asked me: 'For one who practices the Great Way, what is the most urgent matter?'"
"Have you not fallen back into cause and effect? The man replied, "I do not fall into cause and effect," and consequently fell among the wild foxes for five hundred lifetimes.
Now he requests the Master to provide a turning phrase on his behalf. The Master said, "Ask me. The old man said:
"Does a person of great cultivation still fall within cause and effect, or not? Baizhang replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect.
Upon these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.
Whether it be "not falling" or "not obscuring"—if there were even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy between these two statements by Baizhang, an iron mountain would stand across the path.
Have you not seen how, in the past, a man at Lantian shot a tiger? At first, a single arrow sank into its feathers;
upon closer inspection, it was revealed to have been a stone. When he sought to shoot again, the arrow would not penetrate; nearly did he frighten General Li to death.
For a thousand ages, it has caused people to sigh in vain.
Master Tianyi Huai was invited to Shanshan in Chizhou. Upon first entering the monastery, he ascended the hall and said:
"For twenty years I have delighted in longing for this mountain; today, I am truly glad that the conditions have converged. Before I reached this mountain..."
My body arrived at this mountain first; yet when I actually reached it, Shanshan was already within my own body.
Shifting the body and changing the step, the Old Heavenly Ruler’s robe is worn without sparing a single eyebrow—how many truly know?
If today you can clarify the events of that day, the sun is warm in Jiangnan and the partridges cry.
Yunmen said, "A patch-robed monk must have a 'handle' (a point of mastery) before he can recognize people throughout the world.
What is the patch-robed monk’s handle? In response, he said, "Deshan."
On Yunmen’s tongue lies Dragon Spring; he loves to pierce the dark with a golden needle.
If you wish to understand the monk’s nostrils, two people pull at a single red thread.
Once, there was an old woman who took one hundred taels of silver and invited Master Zhaozhou to read a complete collection of the scriptures for her.
Upon receiving the offering, Zhaozhou descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "Give word to the old lady that the reading of the scriptures is finished.
When the old woman heard this, she said, "I have been asking him to read a complete collection; why has he only read half?"
Descending from the meditation seat and walking one circuit, he has read the five thousand scrolls of the Tathāgata. Though the old woman’s years are advanced, her eyesight remains clear;
deep in the night under the moon, she threads her needle.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited Master Fu to lecture on the sutras. As soon as the Master ascended the high seat, he struck the lectern once and immediately descended.
The Emperor was astonished. Master Zhi asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand.
Master Zhi said, "The Master’s lecture on the sutras is finished."
When the Great Being finished lecturing on the sutra, he struck the desk, thereby composing his commentary. A single pill cures all ailments; there is no need for donkey- or camel-carrying medicines.
Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Have you been here before? The monk said, "I have. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea.
He asked another monk, "Have you been here before? The monk said, "I have not. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea. The temple administrator...
Question: "Master, did you go there before? 'Go for tea'—did you not go there before? 'Go for tea'—what is the meaning of this?
The Governor called the head monk. The head monk responded. The Governor said, "Go for tea."
"Once you have arrived, go drink tea; before you have arrived, go drink tea. Old Chan Master Zhaozhou—his mouth scrapes while his heart suffers.
His heart suffers; even until now, there is no place for the snow to melt.
The scholar Zhang Zhuo, while reading the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*, asked Master Changsha Cen:
"I have heard the names of hundreds of thousands of buddhas, but I do not know in what lands they dwell. Cen said:

"After Cui Hao inscribed his verse at the Yellow Crane Tower, did you, scholar, ever write one yourself? Zhuo replied: "I have never written one. Cen said: "If you have nothing else to do, you might as well write one."
Take one verse:
"The waters of the sea, though vast, may at times reveal their depths; But a person from birth until death remains ignorant of their own mind.
If a scholar understands this turning-over phrase, He shall surely be invested in white robes and enter the Hanlin Academy."
Prime Minister Pei was dispatched to serve as a regional governor in Shiling. While visiting Kaiyuan Temple, he saw portraits of eminent monks painted on the walls.
He then asked the monk in charge, "The countenances of these eminent monks are truly worthy of admiration; I wonder, however, where these eminent monks are now. At that time—
The monastic official did not know how to respond. The Duke asked, "Is there any Chan monk here?

The official replied, "Recently there was a monk who abandoned his body to sweep the ground and wore a hundred-patch robe; it might be him. When he was invited to come, it turned out to be Chan Master Huangbo Duanji Yun.
Prime Minister Pei then recounted the previous conversation and questioned Huangbo. Huangbo then called out to him.
"Lord," [Yangshan] called out. "Yes, Lord," [Xuefeng] responded. Yangshan said, "What is it? At these words, the Lord attained a great awakening.
The precious sword of Fengcheng has been buried for a long time; A single beam of cold light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox constellations.
Had it not been for Zhang Hua’s discernment of its true nature, It would have remained a mere blade of grass, wasted for a thousand ages.
One day, while Guishan was seated, Yangshan entered from outside. Guishan clasped his two hands into fists, crossed them, and showed them to him.
Yangshan then performed a woman’s bow. Guishan said, "So it is, so it is."
The beautiful lady, eighteen years of age, is at the height of her youthful charm. She performs a single dance of the *Zhazhi* before the hall;
only Wulang understands her refined grace—no one else can say her willows are like eyebrows.
Xuefeng said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the flames. Yunmen said:
"The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time; the Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen."
Who has trodden upon the tracks of Xuefeng? The Buddhas of the three periods dwell amidst flames. Fortunately, Yunmen provides the warmth;
blowing upon the fire-house, he makes the entire hall crimson.
Master Shushan held a wooden snake in his hand. A monk asked, "What is that in your hand?
Shushan raised it and said, "A girl from the Cao family."
In separation, one’s face is not as radiant as a flower in bloom; in the pain of parting, it is difficult to remain as heartless as a bamboo stalk.
Because others spoke of the lady of the Cao family, my longing has been induced, causing my sickness of love to deepen further.
Laywoman Pang entered Lumeng Monastery to perform a vegetarian feast. The *vinaya-dhara* requested her to dedicate the merit through a formal statement (*shu*).
Laywoman Pang took up a comb, stuck it behind her hair, and said, "The dedication has been made. She then departed.
Pangpo shifts the comb from the side of her topknot; a single stroke of elegance, peerless in all the world. In all matters, simply judge with impartiality;
the rector need not record it in writing.
At Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, [the Buddha] entered meditative absorption. The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī [to act].
With a single snap of his fingers, the woman... King Brahmā fell down from the heavens.
When one Mañjuśrī emerged from this samādhi, ten billion Mañjuśrīs also emerged.
Before he had finished speaking these words of emerging from the samādhi, Jālinīprabha circumambulated the woman.
"□□□□□□□□□□□□ said: 'Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas.
Why was he unable to emerge from the woman's samādhi? Why, then, was Jālinīprabha able to emerge? "
The rolling waves of the Yangtze River are like silver; in autumn days, white artemisia and red smartweed flourish anew. Do not wonder why my small boat finds it difficult to reach the shore;
the movement of the vessel depends entirely upon the person gripping the oar.
Baizhang went for a second audience with Mazu. Mazu held up a fly-whisk. Baizhang said, "Using it right here, yet detached from using it.
Mazu hung the fly-whisk back in its original place. [Baizhang]—Mazu said, "In the future, when you open your two flaps of skin, what will you use to teach people?
Baizhang took up the fly-whisk and held it upright. Mazu said, "Using it right here, yet detached from using it. Baizhang—
He hung the whisk back in its original place. [The text is missing characters here. Huangbo said, "At that time, I was struck by Mazu’s single shout;
it left me deaf for three days."
Father and son meet; their nature is one and the same. The precious sword of Longquan is ground once more.
To clarify Mazu’s shout of that day—throughout the great earth and its mountains and rivers, all are deafened.
Master Shushan asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Lingnan.
Shushan said, "Have you ever been to Xuefeng? The monk said, "I have. Shushan said, "When I went there previously, things were not sufficient;
how are they now? The monk said, "Now they are sufficient. Shushan said, "Sufficient porridge, sufficient rice. The monk was speechless. — Yunmen.
The Master said: "The porridge is finished.
A single imperial highway stretches out level and smooth; countless travelers pass along it at their leisure. Do not say that because the ground is level there is no danger;
you must know that even on level ground there are deep pits."
A monk asked Master Yunmen, “What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing? The Master said, “The seventeenth.
Another monk asked Nanquan, “What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing? Nanquan said, “It was cold, and I had no blanket to cover me.”
One person is skilled at climbing a pole; another is skilled at drilling through a well. Though their skills differ, they all suffer from the same malady.
If one can recognize this malady, the nostrils of all patch-robed monks will be thoroughly pierced.
When Jiashan first resided at Helin Temple in Jingkou, Runzhou, Daowu arrived. Upon encountering him as he was ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body?
Jiashan replied, "The Dharma-body is formless. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-eye?"
Jiashan said, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw. Daowu could not help but let out a laugh.
Jiashan descended from his seat and invited Daowu, saying, "In the dialogue you just had with that monk, there must have been some point where you were incorrect.
I hope you will show me your compassion and instruct me. Daowu said, "I will certainly not say anything here. I invite you to go to Huating in Xiu Prefecture to see Master Huichao."

When Master Heshang of Ship saw Jia Shan, he immediately asked, "Where does the Venerable One reside? Jia Shan replied, "I do not reside in a temple; were I to reside, it would not be like that. The Master of the Boat said, "You say it is not like that—what is it that it is not like? Jia Shan replied, "It is not the Dharma before one's eyes. The Master of the Boat asked, "Where did you learn this? Jia Shan replied, "From nowhere. The Master of the Boat said, "If so, why do you still call yourself a monk? Jia Shan replied, "Because I have no other alternative. The Master of the Boat said, "I am an old man who has traveled far; I must go now. He then departed. Jia Shan followed him for some distance and called out, "Old man! Wait a moment! The Master of the Boat turned his head and looked back. Jia Shan said, "The blue mountains are moving. The Master of the Boat said, "Blue mountains do not move; it is your boat that moves. Jia Shan said, "Whether the mountains move or the boat moves, I do not know. The Master of the Boat said, "Since you do not even know whether the mountains move or the boat moves, how can you claim to be a monk? Jia Shan then returned. Later, when the Master of the Boat reached the monastery, he went straight to the abbot’s quarters and asked, "Where is the Venerable Jia Shan? The abbot replied, "He has already left. The Master of the Boat said, "Tell him I shall see him again on the road. The abbot asked, "What did he say? The Master of the Boat recounted the entire conversation. The abbot said, "That fellow has great capacity; he will surely become a person of great renown. The Master of the Boat said, "He is indeed a vessel for the Dharma.
