Mount Yun said, "It is not something reached by the ears or eyes. Huian the Boatman said, "A single phrase that hits the mark is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.
A line of a thousand feet—the intent lies in the deep pool. Three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak?
As Jia Shan was about to open his mouth, Huian struck him and pushed him into the water. Just as he was about to emerge, Huian said again, "Speak! Speak!"
As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, Huichang struck him again. Jiashan attained a sudden, great enlightenment and nodded his head three times.
Huichang said, "The line on the tip of the pole is for you to play with; it does not offend the clear waves, and its meaning is naturally distinct.
Jiashan asked, "When casting the line and throwing the hook, what is your intention, Master? Huichang said, "The line hangs in the green water, floating steadily."
[The Master] had the intention of [testing] whether [the student] possessed [this realization]. "Quickly speak! Quickly speak! Jia Shan said, "The words carry the profound, yet there is no path;
the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak. Huian (Huangbo) said, "Having fished through the waves of the river, only then is the golden-scaled fish encountered.
Jia Shan then covered his ears. Huian said, "So it is, so it is."

The Dharma-body is without form; the Dharma-eye is without flaw. Like wind fanning a fire, like water used to offer flowers—there is not a hair’s breadth of establishment, yet there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences.
Just wait until the second or third month of next year, when the mud-scarabbing swallow enters the human dwelling.
Jingqing asked a monk, "What is that sound outside the gate? The monk replied, "The sound of raindrops dripping from the eaves. Jingqing said, "Sentient beings are inverted;
deluded about themselves, they pursue external objects."
Raindrops fall from the eaves; the ground before the steps is damp. Every dharma is manifest and complete; yet people do not believe it. What more can be said?
The waters of the Chang Jiang flow swiftly.
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? Dongshan said, "Three pounds of hemp.
Dongshan’s "three pounds of hemp"—the weight does not deceive anyone. The words are sparse, yet the matter is difficult to question; the appearance is ancient, yet the spirit is easily transmitted.
One day, while Yunmen was carrying firewood, he saw a monk drop a piece of wood and said, "The entire Tripitaka speaks only of this.
Xuansha said, "The entire Tripitaka does not speak of this."
In every place, green willows are fit for tethering horses; at every household, the gateways lead straight through to Chang’an. This one great road is as level as the palm of a hand;
it is simply that people of this age find it difficult to set foot upon it.
A monk asked an old woman, "Where does the road to Mount Tai lead? The woman said, "Go straight ahead.
As soon as the monk took a step, she said, "What a fine master you are, yet you go off like that. Whenever he questioned her in this manner, she always answered in the same way.
The monk related this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Wait; let me examine and expose this old woman for you.
He then went to ask her, "Which way does the road to Mount Tai go? The woman replied, "Go straight ahead.
Just as Zhaozhou began to walk, the woman said, "What a fine master you are, yet you still go that way! Zhaozhou returned and told the assembly, "I have examined and exposed this..."
"An old wife indeed. The Elder took up the case and said: "Where is the point of his being thoroughly tested?
Go straight ahead! Go straight ahead! Countless people have their sandals' heels worn through. To sing the song, one must be a man from the Imperial Capital."
One claps and one dances; when the dance is complete, there is nothing more to it. Master Zhaozhou and the old woman used this specifically to deceive.
From ancient times to the present, the road beneath Mount Wutai has long pines and short cypresses soaring toward the clouds.
Once, while Mazu was gazing at the moon with Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan, Mazu asked Baizhang, "At this very moment, what is it?
Baizhang replied, "It is precisely the time for making offerings. He then asked Xitang, who said, "It is precisely the time for practicing the Way.
Nanquan, however, shook his sleeves and walked away. Mazu remarked, "The sutras have entered the canon; Chan has returned to the sea. Only Nanquan remains."
Vow: To transcend all things alone.
Mazu held forth the rhombus-patterned mirror; Old Wang personally took up the white jade mallet. With one strike in the presence of all, the tiles were shattered.
How many can truly know this mind? How many know it? Two are clearly the "Red Eyebrows" (the rebel leaders). Before the wind—
Revealing the family’s disgrace under the moon, he makes the ancient adept of Vulture Peak laugh until he falls over.
Zhaozhou visited a certain hermitage master and asked, “Is there anything here? Is there anything here? The master raised his fist.
Zhaozhou said, “The water is too shallow; it is no place to moor a boat,” and he departed. He then visited another hermitage master and asked him the same thing: “Is there anything here?”
"Is there such a thing? The Abbot again raised his fist. Zhaozhou said, "He can bestow and he can seize; he can kill and he can bring to life. Having paid his respects, he departed.

When he went up to the hermitage, the Abbot raised his fist; Zhaozhou said, "The left eye is half a catty. When he went down from the hermitage, the Abbot raised his fist; Zhaozhou said, "The right eye is eight ounces. Zhaozhou then departed.
Eight *liang* in the right eye. Look at the Iron Ox of Shanfu—how does it compare to the Great Image of Jiazhou?
If you say there is no confusion or contradiction whatsoever, then the pillar and the lantern will join their palms.
A monk asked Master Yunmen, "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? Yunmen said, "A sesame cake.
Yunmen’s single sesame cake has been chewed by the monks of the world; were it not for those with iron-jawed teeth, they would often—
Swallow it whole. It is easy to swallow, but difficult to spit out. Do not say that it has always been like ordinary flour;
only by treading upon the pivot of Shaoyang can one stir up waves upon level ground.
One day, while Zhaozhou was in his quarters, a novice monk announced the arrival of the assembly. Zhaozhou said to his attendant, "Send him away.
As soon as the attendant told him to leave, the novice simply said, "Goodbye" (*zhēnzhòng*). Zhaozhou then said to a nearby monk, "The novice has entered the gate;
the attendant remains outside it."
Zhaozhou’s gate has no locks at all. The attendant was careless and missed it head-on. The sharp-witted śrāmaṇera took his leave with care.
The Master said, "Is there a turning word for this point? After a long silence, no one responded. The Master said, "It is late;
go back to the hall and warm yourselves by the fire."
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
Zhaozhou’s cypress in the courtyard—how does it compare to the willow outside the gate? The large month has thirty days; the small month has twenty-nine.
He asked again how the matter was; [the master] closed his mouth as if it were a living one.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "Hiding one's body within the Northern Dipper."
The Northern Dipper conceals its body; to deliberate upon it is immediately erroneous. A new hawk piercing the heavens has no lingering attachment to its former nest.
Yunmen once said: "The lantern is your own self; taking up the alms bowl to eat rice is not your own self.
A monk asked: "If eating rice were one's own self, what then? Yunmen said: "This wild fox spirit! (3)
A man from a rustic village. Baizhang said, "Come, come. [The monk] said, "You say that food is for oneself. The monk said, "Yes.
Baizhang said, "In donkey-years you will dream of a man from a rustic village."
All morning long they spend their efforts eating rice; they do not realize that the lantern is the alms bowl.
How many men from the three-family village are there, busily trying to catch catfish on a tree!
A monk asked Master Rang: "When a mirror casts an image, once the image has been formed, where does the light go? Rang replied:
"When you, Venerable Sir, had not yet left the household life, where did your physical form go? The monk asked: "Once [the image] is formed, why does it no longer reflect?
Rang replied: "Although... (The text here is fragmentary).
The eyes within the skull are still visible; the dragon’s roar from within the withered tree is even more frantic.
When the void is shattered and the realm of light is exhausted, there is something else to be deliberated within this.
The Master held up the incense and said: "Recalling last year’s spring, at this very season, my two fists shattered the vast void, and countless family traditions were completely revealed.
The lion among men lost his full stature; the qilin in the moonlight broke its horns.
Its horns broken, the adamantine true eye remains indestructible. For a thousand ages it causes people to recite it without ceasing. He blew [on the incense].
"A single speck of cloud scattered over the red furnace.
The Master again called to the assembly, saying: "Do not blame the house for not being broken; it is because the people within have not yet grown great.

A single mother gives birth to children of a hundred different kinds; who would have known that the ancestral estate of Chan Master Jingzhao would reach Zifu and be swept away until nothing remained? Nevertheless..."
It is thus: opening the mouth to eat rice, raising the hand to put on clothes, and emerging from within the gate—these are not yet the work of a master.
To establish one’s livelihood upon level ground and to devise a means of subsistence within empty space—only when one emerges from within the body is one truly a man of substance.
Speaking in such a manner—who among you is a true connoisseur? To examine this matter closely, it is much like broadcasting one's own family’s disgrace and inviting derision from others.
Is there anyone here, among you, who, upon hearing of a death in the eastern house, would go to the western house to offer condolences? If there is no such person...
"I, this mountain monk, cannot help but weep for myself. The Master covered his face with his hand and wept, saying, "Heaven! Heaven! On the anniversary of his passing, he offered incense, saying:
"In a single word our paths met; like water and milk, we were in harmony. We followed one another through three places; master and disciple were in perfect accord."
Where others are earnest and grasping, Zifu knows it all; where Zifu is lame and stumbling, others see it all.
Sometimes, at the bottom of a thousand-fathom sea, we walk hand in hand; sometimes, atop a hundred-foot pole, he turns his body and plunges straight down.
Those who can see him truly find it difficult to forget until their dying day; those who cannot see him remain so even to this day.
He still harbors a sense of resentment. This mountain monk’s own heart and mind are perfectly clear; there is nothing in my heart that I owe anyone.

Therefore, whenever I arrive at the anniversary of his passing, I cannot help but prepare an offering for him and burn a stick of incense. Although worldly conventions have not yet been forgotten, [this is how it is].
Furthermore, I wish to leave everyone in a state of suspended animation. He then looked toward the assembly and said: "The burning of incense and the setting out of offerings are known to all of you.
But tell me, how do you express the phrase 'the mind that does not betray others'? After a long silence, he said: "Each time one drinks water, each time one chokes;
fundamentally without sentiment, yet appearing to have sentiment. If you wish to understand the definitive meaning within this, listen as the wooden cock crows."
Two kinds of sounds.

On the anniversary of [the Master’s]忌辰 (memorial day), he offered incense and said: "This matter has been transmitted for eight hundred years; in truth, there is not a single dharma to be passed on to others.
Today, wishing to repay that which cannot be transmitted, I shall briefly burn a single incense stick in this golden censer. He then added: "Even so, it is burned away—what is the meaning?"
This was also not yet clarified. I recall that one day Master Dongshan was preparing a vegetarian feast for Chan Master Yunyan Cheng.
A monk asked, "When you were at Yunyan’s place, what instruction did you receive? Dongshan said, "Although I was there, I did not receive his instruction.
The monk said, "If you did not receive his instruction, why are you now preparing a feast for him? Dongshan—
The monk said, "How would I dare disobey him? The monk asked, "In years past, you set out from Nanquan;
for what reason did you instead receive Dharma succession from Yunyan? Mountains said, "I do not value my late teacher’s moral virtue or his Buddha-dharma;
I only value that he did not explain it through for me. The monk asked, "I wonder, did he approve of you or not? Mountains said, "Half approved, half not approved. The monk—
[The Master] asked, "Why do you not fully agree? Shan said, "If I were to fully agree, I would be failing my late teacher.

The Master said, "Old man Dongshan seems to have failed to consider the consequences of his actions; he merely labors in regret. Since the nose has already fallen into the hands of others, what does it matter whether one agrees half or fully?
Whether one explains it through or does not explain it through—O Great Man, you must simply cut it with a single stroke."
The debt of gratitude is clearly repaid. Nevertheless, there is one phrase that I shall now reveal to this old fellow.
After a long silence, he said: "Who knows that within the thousand-year belly of this old fellow, there lies a bright pearl ten inches in diameter?"

When Chan Master Dengyun entered the coffin, the Master struck the coffin with his hand and said, "The assembly, the Buddhas of antiquity departed in this manner; the Buddhas of the present depart in this manner."
Master Dengyun also departed in this manner. What thing does not decay? Who remains eternally firm?
Do you all know where Dengyun has gone? If you do, then the entire assembly at Jiaoshan enters nirvana together with Dengyun.
If it is not yet so, then the stone man with eyes sheds tears in unison, and the mute child sighs in secret.
As Chan Master Dengyuncong was consigning [the remains] to the flames, the Master held up a torch and said: "Do you know where this old fellow has traveled throughout his life?
Before Mount Huiri, he revealed his true face through a thousand lifetimes; beneath Mount Shigong, he once spread out a single leaf as a compassionate vessel. His tune is ancient and his spirit..."

The pure breeze rises from on high; his appearance is haggard, yet his bones are firm—people pay him no heed. In years past, he shook out his sleeves and departed; who could vie with him for the wind and moon over the Five Lakes? Today he returns once more;
it was never that he would not return, for upon returning, he finds his way. Now he rejoices in gathering his line and laying down his hook, reclining in the western hermitage.
Who would have expected that the leaves fall back to their root, and he hides himself within the Northern Dipper? To be thus, to be thus—is this it? No.
"Whether it be thus or not thus is difficult. A steel ox is mounted backward upon Mount Sumeru; a jade flute is blown crosswise, resounding through the azure void.
Such skillful means can only be known by a true master. Raising your eyebrows, I ask you to open your eyes wide.
Today, for the sake of Old Man Dengyun, I shall speak a final word that outshines the past and leaves nothing behind. Thereupon, he took a torch and circled the shrine.
After circumambulating once, he said: "If you call this 'fire,' it is like seeing ghosts before a skull;
if you do not call it 'fire,' it is like deceiving people behind a pillar. Tell me, ultimately how is it? The Master smiled and said: "Who knows this meaning?
It makes me recall my days atop Yunmen Peak."

This old fellow, Master Shengcheng, who performed the cremation rites, was at that time withered and parched; he did not conform to worldly sentiments. He stood alone as a solitary beacon throughout the four seas, with no companion for his single body.
Although he held the patriarchal seal in both hands, in truth he bestowed not a single dharma upon others. He sat upright in his inner chamber, cold and silent.
In the stillness of night, I speak alone to the ghosts and spirits. Let bystanders vent their malice as they will; my heart remains ultimately unconciliated.
At times I open my eyes to face the green mountains and laugh at myself for the white hair growing on my head. To those who do not know me, it seems I am out of step with the times.
To those who do know me, there is only Mount Jiao; I can no longer form worldly ties. It is all the same—I simply must.
"Traveling the path beyond. Now tell me, what is this path beyond? After a long silence, he said:
"To topple the shadowless tree before the cliff, one must be able to turn somersaults within the flames."

When the practitioners of dhyāna send down the fire at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, many patch-robed monks wish to depart. They do not board old-fashioned boats, but instead set out on the road to Sizhou.
With staff slung across their shoulders and a breath like clouds, they heed neither ten thousand waters nor a thousand mountains. Yesterday, they arrived at Tongchuan.
Entering. Following the pattern, it is vast and boundless; one cannot hold onto it. One cannot hold onto it. For your sake, I shall speak a verse for the parting of the ways:
Before the withered tree at the crag, divergent paths abound; raise your eyebrows and look with your own eyes.
This single body is as fleeting as a candle in the wind; a hundred years are but bubbles upon the water.

Until one reaches the stable ground of the patch-robed monk, how could one avoid feeling sorrow at the time of departure? If you wish to avoid such sorrow, attend to the affairs of a busy time while you are still at leisure.

Look! Clouds gather over the vast fields; snow accumulates across the long plains. At such a time, people lose their way and cannot find the traces of the path, yet this monk possesses a road that pierces the heavens.
Let us not speak of the realm of Samantabhadra; you must know that within this single color there is no difference.
Do you all understand how this monk and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra move with sovereign ease through this world of silver? At this moment—
If you do not seek out his traces, you will not meet him even if you go to Mount Emei.
This floating life is like a tree on the riverbank or a vine by a well; in the end, it inevitably returns to decay.
This monk, tossing up his robe and walking away, was truly joyful throughout his life. Putting on his bottomless straw sandals and casting off this skin-bag—tell me, what about the Vinaya?
When a person casts aside this skin-sack, where will they go? Only when poverty comes does one realize that money is what can be used;
only after waking does one know that wine has deceived the person.
The tea stove in the Dharma Hall is still burning; another person has passed away in the Yan-shou Hall. To speak plainly, this body is entirely empty and void. All things are like a single dream.
Thus we know that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are also a dream, and the six generations of patriarchs are also a dream.
This monk has finished his dreaming. I dare ask you all: tell me, what did he see in his dream?
[He] said, "Mò. After a long silence, he said: "Thirty-four years have passed like the turning of a palm. The dream of returning to Qiāntáng has ended at this moment.
Water remains unchanged; earth and water divide and flow around. All things are not solid; where does the single spiritual essence go?
To say that fundamentally there is no birth or death is merely the style of a lecturer. To further say it does not belong to coming or going is not yet the realm of a patch-robed monk."
Ultimately, how shall one deliberate upon this? After a long silence, he said: "Night travel is not permitted;
at dawn, you must arrive. This matter, from antiquity to the present day, who has been able to escape it?

If you have never yet stepped upon the ground of the Patriarchs, then even if your rhetoric is as brilliant as dew and your eloquence like a shower of pearls—your nostrils reaching to the heavens and your spirit piercing the Ox and Dipper constellations—it will be of no avail.
"Arriving at such a place as this, there is nowhere for you to escape. Why is it so? 'Much emptiness is not as good as little reality.
The practitioner descends into the fire."
"You entered the Gate of Emptiness in your youth; now, at the age of twenty-five, before your beard and hair have even been removed, your illusory body departs today.
Cast off your plain cotton robe; do not ask for the way to Wenzhou. Tell me, Great Assembly: since you do not ask for the way to Wenzhou, [where are you going?]"
"Where are you going? You cannot stay where there is a Buddha; you must run swiftly past where there is no Buddha.
Master Tianliu Nüzi, while lighting the firebrand, said: "Do you see it? Only after thirty-two years of this floating life did I finally begin to practice."
If you are willing to turn your head, this matter will again vanish like clouds and rain; the misty waves upon the river make one sorrowful. Rest, rest, rest! There is no need for sorrow.
Meeting and parting are just like bubbles upon the water. Even if one were to live for thirty years, one cannot avoid losing this single point to him.
Lady Tianliu, on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month, she lost this single point to him.
Is there anyone who can still save you? I borrow for you a single torch of light to shatter the body of the five hindrances that have persisted since the past.
(The wife and daughter of Ding Zhongxun descend together into the fire.)
"For over twenty years I have dwelt here; weeds and dust have obscured my youthful countenance.
This morning, mother and child should congratulate one another, for we joyfully welcome the spring’s return to our old pass. He then addressed the assembly again:

"Two caskets of bleached bones, a single torch of crimson flame—soon they shall turn to ash. How can you explain the principle of 'returning to the old pass'? After a long silence, he said: "The wilds."
The fire cannot burn it away; when the spring breeze blows, it grows anew.
Master Wei descended from the pyre—alas for Wei Dahe!
